items.title: Philippine Police Arrest 11 Indigenous Rights Protesters
items.description: Click to expand Image Indigenous residents from Nueva Vizcaya province protest outside the Mines and Geosciences Bureau and the Department of Environment and Natural Resources in Quezon City, Philippines, on July 13, 2026. © 2026 Charles Edmon Perez/JNA Press/Sipa USA via AP Photo Philippine police on August 28 dispersed a barricade that Indigenous communities had erected in Kasibu town, Nueva Vizcaya province, and arrested 11 Indigenous protesters. Members of the Bugkalot/Ilangot and other tribes have peacefully maintained a barricade since May to oppose the exploration activities of North Luzon Mineral Resources Corporation. Videos and photos posted on social media show more than a dozen police officers breaking up the barricade by handcuffing residents, including older people. A 63-year-old man fainted as he was arrested by police and was taken to the hospital. Police pinned one resident to the ground. Prosecutors charged the protesters with “grave coercions” and “resistance and disobedience to people in authority” under the Philippines revised penal code, which carries a sentence of one to six months’ imprisonment. All were released on bail on September 1. North Luzon Mineral Resources Corporation has an exploration permit granted on June 25, 2025, and has said it has a certification from the Philippine National Commission on Indigenous Peoples that its permit area does not overlap with customary land. Community residents who oppose the company’s activities have said they have a Certificate of Land Ownership Award that confirms their land rights. They have filed a petition before the Department of Environment and Natural Resources to cancel the exploration permit it granted to the company. Two community leaders and two of their lawyers are facing cyber-libel complaints filed by the North Luzon Mineral Resources Corporation. The cyber-libel charge against the lawyers effectively undermines their right to freedom of expression and to fully represent their clients in accordance with the United Nations Basic Principles on the Role of Lawyers. Residents have been trying to prevent the entry of equipment and fuel into the drilling site. A truck carrying fuel for a local road project was stopped at the barricade by the residents on August 18, and police arrested three Indigenous protesters, who were later released on bail. Philippine authorities should drop criminal charges against community members exercising their right to peaceful assembly and expression. The Philippine government should instead seriously address the conflicting land claims that underlie the dispute.

Cases à étage de Mlomp : un patrimoine qui attire les touristes
items.description: Inscrites depuis le début des années 2000 sur la liste du patrimoine historique du Sénégal, les maisons à étage de Mlomp suscitent la curiosité. Ces bâtiments inspirés des tirailleurs sénégalais font de Mlomp une étape incontournable des circuits touristiques de la Casamance. OUSSOUYE – Sur la route d’Elinkine, à hauteur de la place publique de Djicomole (quartier de Mlomp), se dressent deux édifices construits sur deux niveaux. Il s’agit des étages de Mlomp, situés en plein cœur du Kassa (département d’Oussouye). Ces maisons, construites à côté de fromagers centenaires, sont une singularité architecturale qui attire. Les touristes sénégalais et étrangers, qui empruntent cette voie pour aller à la pointe Saint-Georges ou dans l’île de Casamance, font un arrêt devant ces joyaux pour contempler le génie architectural diola. Certains s’offrent même le privilège de visiter l’intérieur des bâtiments. « Les maisons ont été faites avec essentiellement des matériaux locaux », explique Léon Abeudj, guide touristique originaire de la commune de Mlomp. Une inspiration européenne adaptée à la créativité locale Ces maisons communément appelées étages en banco, poursuit-il, ont été construites sans fer ni ciment. « Les murs ont été faits avec de l’argile et du bois. Le plafond avec des tiges de palétuviers », souligne Lamine Diop Sané qui organise régulièrement des visites guidées sur ces lieux devenus incontournables pour les touristes. Le président des guides touristiques de la Casamance renseigne que l’ingéniosité utilisée garantit la durabilité des maisons et leur confère une température moins rude, quelle que soit la période de l’année. Au-delà de leur symbole esthétique, les maisons à étages de Mlomp traduisent un mariage architectural entre l’Occident et l’Afrique. « Les plans sont une inspiration européenne. Mais les techniques de construction sont purement locales », explique Gustave Bénédicte Sarr, enseignant. Le natif du village de Kagnout renseigne que les premiers bâtiments dans ce style ont été construits après la Première Guerre mondiale (1914-1918). A lire aussi : Jean-Pierre Gomis, dit Agolène : Le bâtisseur de l’île de Djirouatou « C’est quand nos aïeux qui ont participé à cette guerre sont revenus qu’ils ont voulu reproduire ce qu’ils ont vu en France. Mais comme à cette époque il n’y avait ni de ciment, encore moins de fer, ils ont su compenser avec les matériaux locaux », mentionne le secrétaire chargé du patrimoine et des sociocultures de l’association des acteurs culturels du département d’Oussouye, par ailleurs conservateur du musée de Kagnout. Les maisons à étages du genre, le village de Mlomp en compte un peu moins d’une dizaine. La plupart sont habitées par les descendants des tirailleurs sénégalais. Elles mettent en exergue la capacité d’adaptation et de créativité des populations locales et témoignent aussi de l’expérience des anciens combattants ayant sué et versé leur sang pour défendre la France, ancienne puissance coloniale, contre l’Allemagne nazie. Par Kathafa B.H.M. KANFOUDY (correspondant)

items.title: Kloto/Social : L’ONG CITAPA remet des allocations aux orphelins
items.description: Kpalimé, 3 sept. (ATOP) – L’ONG Centre Ibn Taimiyah pour la prédication et Al-Ifta (CITAPA) a remis symboliquement des allocations aux orphelins, le mercredi 2 septembre à Kpalimé, pour l’année scolaire 2026-2027. A travers cette initiative, L’ONG CITAPA et ses partenaires arabes qui ont mobilisé 39 117 418 FCFA pour 567 orphelins de différentes localités du Togo entendent contribuer à la prise en charge des besoins des enfants orphelins et à leur maintien dans le système éducatif. Au cours de cette cérémonie, certains orphelins ont reçu directement leur assistance. Les allocations des autres bénéficiaires, ont été transférées sur leurs comptes bancaires. Remise d’une vache à un bénéficiaire Les responsables de CITAPA ont invité les parents et tuteurs à consacrer ces allocations à la scolarisation des bénéficiaires et, lorsque cela est possible, à l’apprentissage d’un métier. Les intervenants leur ont demandé d’éviter toute utilisation des fonds qui ne contribuerait pas directement au bien-être et à l’avenir des enfants. Le représentant du préfet de Kloto, M. Koudjo Kodjo, a estimé que cette initiative contribue à redonner espoir aux enfants orphelins et à compléter les efforts des pouvoirs publics en matière d’assistance aux personnes démunies. La représentante du maire de Kloto 1, Mme Koudouremé Egoulou, a appelé les bénéficiaires à faire un bon usage des allocations. Elle a également exhorté les enfants à prendre au sérieux leurs études afin de pouvoir, à terme, contribuer au développement de leur communauté. La rencontre a également été marquée par la remise de 10 vaches à dix personnes nécessiteuses de Kpalimé et de Sokodé pour leur permettre de développer des activités d’élevage. Ces animaux ne sont destinés ni à la vente ni à l’abattage, a précisé le président de CITAPA, Abdoulahi Mouhamed Yolou. Les bénéficiaires pourront notamment tirer profit du lait, soit pour leur consommation, soit pour sa commercialisation, afin de contribuer aux charges de leurs ménages. Créée en 2003, l’ONG CITAPA est une organisation religieuse non gouvernementale dont le siège se trouve à Kpalimé. Elle intervient notamment dans le parrainage des orphelins, l’assistance aux veuves et aux personnes vulnérables, la construction de maisons pour les veuves, la réalisation de forages et la construction de centres de formation. ATOP/ER/AYH/OA

items.description: El líder del PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, ha reclamado la dimisión del presidente del Gobierno “por incompetente o por cómplice” y ha asegurado que “pagará ante la justicia”. Lo ha hecho en respuesta a la intervención de Sánchez, quien ha explicado ante el Pleno la gestión de la crisis desde la entrada masiva de más de 80.000 personas los pasados 30 y 31 de julio. El presidente ha anunciado que el Gobierno convocó el pasado 21 de agosto a la embajadora de Marruecos, Karima Benyaich, por declaraciones “inaceptables” de dos ministros marroquíes sobre Ceuta y Melilla, y que modificará la cooperación con Marruecos para reforzar los mecanismos de alerta. Ha negado que el Ejecutivo recibiera “alertas o avisos extraordinarios” antes de la entrada masiva y ha anunciado que publicará un dosier con los informes de aquellos días. Considera necesario, además, que el Rey visite Ceuta y Melilla “en las próximas semanas”, tras 20 años sin hacerlo. En su contrarréplica, Sánchez ha reprochado a Feijóo y al líder de Vox, Santiago Abascal, acusar al Ejecutivo de no proteger las fronteras: “¿Habrían ordenado a la Policía Nacional y a la Guardia Civil disparar a la población civil en el Tarajal? ¿Habrían preferido matar a cientos, quizá miles de jóvenes, muchos de ellos menores, para evitarse gestionar una crisis de acogida?”. items.title: GRIDCo warns encroachers as activities under high-voltage lines threaten power supply
items.description: The Ghana Grid Company Limited (GRIDCo) has warned that illegal structures and human activities along its high-voltage transmission lines pose serious risks to lives and could disrupt electricity supply. The company says increasing encroachment on its transmission right-of-way is creating dangerous conditions that could affect the stability of the national power transmission network. Speaking to JoyNews, GRIDCo’s Director of Corporate Strategy, Samuel Kow Acquah, cited a recent incident at Ashaiman, where a tanker damaged part of a transmission tower, resulting in a prolonged power outage. “We are seeing increasingly human activities such as these encroachments around our right-of-way that potentially could disrupt power supply,” he said. According to him, the incident occurred when a tanker being welded came into contact with the transmission infrastructure. “About two weeks ago, we had a similar incident in Ashaiman where a tanker that was being welded shattered and damaged portions of the transmission tower, and we had to take power out for a number of hours,” Acquah explained. He said GRIDCo is therefore intensifying its education campaign to warn squatters, encroachers and others who have occupied areas within its right-of-way about the dangers their activities pose to human life and electricity supply. “We are using this opportunity to educate all encroachers, squatters and people who have illegally occupied our right-of-way about the dangers of doing this—one, to human life, and also the potential destruction to power supply,” he said. Mr Acquah stressed that GRIDCo was taking technical measures to address bottlenecks within the transmission network and did not want human activities to undermine those efforts. “We are doing everything technically possible to make sure that the bottlenecks within the transmission network are eliminated. The least we want to have is to have human activities such as these disrupt power supply,” he said. The awareness campaign, he noted, will continue throughout the month across regions with high levels of encroachment and illegal mining activities. GRIDCo to Validate Residents’ Claims On concerns raised by some affected residents regarding discussions with government and changes to the transmission lines, Mr Acquah said GRIDCo would validate such claims before taking further action. “The areas that the team have marked, we will come back and then do the validation of these claims by the residents. Of course, there will be a human touch to any exercise that we conduct,” he said. He added that residents who voluntarily vacate the right-of-way would be encouraged to do so, while those who remain after the required notice period could face lawful enforcement action. “Those who will still be here after the notice period, whatever action legally within our rights will be exercised,” Mr Acquah stated. Two-Week Moratorium Mr Acquah disclosed that the two-week moratorium announced by the Minister for Energy Dr John Abdulai Jinapor would expire on September 4, but said affected residents would still be given reasonable notice to vacate the transmission right-of-way before enforcement begins. He further warned that the high voltage carried by the transmission lines makes living or conducting activities within the right-of-way extremely dangerous. “We are talking about a line carrying 161,000 volts and, in some instances, 313,000 volts. In your house, you need just 240 volts to power your equipment,” he said. He explained that activities under the transmission lines could cause electrical induction and potentially lead to a line snapping, creating further problems across the transmission network. “It is really dangerous to occupy the right-of-way and for activities that would potentially cause induction under the right-of-way. These will be very disruptive to power supply,” he cautioned. The campaign is being conducted in collaboration with the Information Services Department and the media, particularly in the Ashanti, Eastern, Bono, Western and Western North regions, where GRIDCo says encroachment and illegal mining activities have been particularly prevalent. Residents Express Concerns Some residents affected by the exercise, however, have raised concerns about the history of the transmission infrastructure in their communities and possible demolition of their properties and businesses. One resident said the transmission poles had previously been located further away from the area but were later moved closer to the community. “We are all worried here because we have been in this area for over 40 years,” the resident said. The resident, however, indicated a willingness to comply if the reasons for the exercise were properly explained. We are ready to comply, if only they reason with us, because we are also doing our business here. Our wives, our brothers and sisters are doing their business here,” the resident added. Another resident expressed concern about the possible demolition of homes and businesses and called for clarity on compensation. “People are worried because you see the houses, all the rooms and all that. I don’t know whether they will do something about that,” the resident said.

items.title: ‘I thought of selling my laptop’ – Ex-BBN star Danboskid opens up on struggles
items.description: Former Big Brother Naija Season 10 housemate, Daniel Olatunji, popularly known as Danboskid, has opened up about his current struggles, revealing plans to rebuild his career and become financially independent. The reality TV star made the disclosure in a video shared on Wednesday, where he spoke candidly about returning to his family home and his efforts to get his life back on track. Danboskid revealed that he is currently staying in his sister’s room while working on several plans aimed at helping him regain his footing. Among his plans are producing a movie, becoming a top actor, starting an accessories business and driving for Uber. "I don’t have anything, just my laptop" — BBNaija's Danboskid speaks on hitting rock bottom and wanting to start over again. pic.twitter.com/cOtavvvMaK — OVA TV MEDIA (@ovatvofficial) September 3, 2026 He also spoke about the difficulties confronting his family, but stressed that he was not looking for sympathy. Instead, he said he needed advice and support as he worked towards changing his circumstances. “I don’t really know what to say, but I know I have so many things in mind. And I know I don’t know what’s going on with me. “But I know I have to change what’s going on. I know I have to stop being intentional. I know I have to start altering my own reality. “Because I have to make things work regardless.” Reflecting further on his situation, Danboskid said his family had not been deprived of basic necessities but admitted that they were experiencing mental and emotional difficulties. “As I said, we’re not suffering. My dad is a tenant. So yeah, we’re just suffering mentally,” he said. The former housemate also revealed that he had contemplated selling his laptop to raise money but ultimately decided to keep it because of its importance to his plans for rebuilding his career. He said one of his major ambitions was to establish himself in the film industry, starting with a movie he is already working on. “I have a script going on. I’m going to produce my movie. I’m going to become a movie producer.And a world-class top actor. “Yes, that’s it. So that’s the first one. That’s like the bigger picture. But how do we go about it? I honestly do not know.” Beyond filmmaking, Danboskid said he was determined to launch an accessories brand, which he hopes will provide another source of income as he works towards becoming financially stable. “I also want to start my accessory brand. “Oh yeah, I know how to select good accessories. “So yeah, you all know I’m going to put on my business page to patronise me because that’s how I want to kick-start myself.” He also disclosed plans to drive for Uber, including the possibility of using vehicles belonging to people who no longer want to operate them themselves. According to the reality star, his immediate priorities are to become independent, secure accommodation and support his family. “Get something done for myself. Start doing Uber. Start my accessory brand. “Get a house for myself. Fix my family, and become a meaningful user. That’s the plan.” Danboskid also spoke about the pressure that comes with being a public figure, saying he wanted to move beyond the image people had formed of him through his online presence. He said he was determined to demonstrate his abilities and pursue opportunities without allowing public perception to define what he could achieve. The reality star was among the housemates who featured in the 2025 edition of BBNaija and was the first contestant evicted from the show. items.title: Why Argentina can’t retire Messi’s number 10 jersey
items.description: By Enitan Abdultawab Lionel Messi may have ended his international career, but Argentina will not be able to permanently withdraw the iconic No. 10 shirt because of FIFA’s regulations on squad numbers. Messi confirmed his decision to step away from international football on August 31, two days after Argentina lost the 2026 FIFA World Cup final to Spain. Although his retirement had been widely anticipated, the announcement officially brought the curtain down on a remarkable international career that saw him win the World Cup in 2022. The Argentina Football Association had previously expressed its desire to retire the No. 10 shirt in honour of Messi. AFA president Claudio Tapia said as far back as 2014 that the number would be retired once the legendary forward ended his international career. However, FIFA regulations prevent national teams from leaving squad numbers permanently unused. The rules require every shirt number within a national team squad to be assigned to a player. Therefore, Argentina would have to give the No. 10 jersey to another player rather than permanently reserve it for Messi. The regulation is not new and had previously affected Diego Maradona. Argentina could not retire the No. 10 shirt after Maradona’s career, allowing Messi to eventually inherit the number and build his own legacy with it. A similar situation has also occurred in club football. Barcelona were unable to permanently withdraw the No. 10 shirt because of La Liga regulations before eventually handing it to Lamine Yamal. Franco Mastantuono was the most recent player to wear Argentina’s No. 10 in Messi’s absence, taking the shirt when the captain missed a match in September 2025. With Messi now out of the national team picture, Como midfielder Nico Paz is among the players being considered to take over the famous number. Inter Milan striker Lautaro Martinez is another possible candidate. Whoever inherits the shirt will face enormous expectations, given the extraordinary legacy Messi leaves behind after wearing No. 10 for Argentina for many years. Messi finished his international career as Argentina’s all-time leading scorer with 125 goals and represented the country at six World Cups. He also led La Albiceleste to the 2022 World Cup title, ending Argentina’s 36-year wait for the trophy. The post Why Argentina can’t retire Messi’s number 10 jersey appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Act for Nutrition conference: Minister stresses need for communication, awareness to tackle malnutrition
items.description: A two-day international conference, ‘Act For Nutrition: The Emergency We Can No Longer Ignore’, held at Islamabad’s Serena Hotel, concluded on Thursday, with experts calling for food and nutritional security to be recognised as fundamental rights. The conference aimed to address Pakistan’s persistent nutrition and stunting crisis. On the first day , experts at the conference warned that more than four in 10 children under five were stunted and malnutrition was costing Pakistan close to $17 billion annually. They also said that malnutrition was produced by a combination of poor diets, inadequate healthcare, weak water and sanitation services, poverty and other factors, making a multisectoral response essential. The two-day conference brought together policymakers, international development leaders, health professionals and nutrition experts to confront the burgeoning crisis and build momentum for urgent, coordinated action. View the full agenda here . 4:55pm - Conference concludes 4:40pm - Malnutrition ‘greatest barrier’ to development: WHO official Representative of the World Health Organisation (WHO) in Pakistan Dr Dapeng Luo, in his closing remarks, stressed that malnutrition remained the “greatest barrier” to health, development, and opportunities. He noted that nutrition was “much more than access to food” and further stated that “predictable and solid regulation” was needed as a way forward. 4:30pm - BNP showed nutrition can be integrated into social protection, says WFP official WFP’s Country Director for Pakistan Anita Hirsch also noted the progress of the Benazir Nashonuma Programme (BNP), which she said had shown that nutrition can be integrated into national social protection. “As we look ahead, one priority is to sustain those gains, continue to scale up and integrate services for millions of Pakistani women and children,” Hirsch said. 4:22pm - WFP official shares her key takeaways World Food Programme’s Country Director for Pakistan Anita Hirsch shared her key takeaways from the two-day conference. “Pakistan continues to face a high level of malnutrition. More than 40pc of children under five are stunted. This means children whose growth and cognitive development are compromised,” Hirsch said. She continued: “Second takeaway was that timing matters; the first 1,000 days represent a critical window that will have lifelong implications for the potential for children and potential for Pakistan, and that adolescence also matters.” Hirsch also noted the economic cost of malnutrition, remarking that it remained a barrier to national growth and prosperity. “17bn dollars are lost every year to malnutrition and stunting,” she said. “My last takeaway was that addressing malnutrition is not just about food alone; it is about health, education, women’s empowerment, behaviour change. “It takes a village; it is our collective responsibility, and it is also a national emergency and one that we must collectively address.” 4:15pm- Expert calls on govt to recognise food and nutritional security as a fundamental right Chairperson SUN Movement Dr Irshad Danish also recommended that the government should recognise food and nutritional security as a fundamental right in the Constitution. “There are some provisions, but nutrition and food security are not fundamental rights,” he said. He also recommended that nutrition should be institutionalised as a sector and stressed the need for multisectoral coordination. 4:10pm - Pakistan’s nutritional burden must be treated as a national emergency, says expert Dr Irshad Danish, who is the chairperson of the Scaling Up Nutrition movement, summarising the two-day conference, said that in the discussions held, it was recognised that “scale and severity of Pakistan’s malnutrition burden must be treated as a national emergency and put forward some recommendations”. Outlining one of the recommendations made, Dr Danish said, “First, we propose and recommend that the government should appoint dedicated nutrition coordinators and focal persons at national and international level”. 4:07pm - Closing session titled ‘Stronger Together — The Pakistan Nutrition Pact’ begins The final session of the day has begun. 3:45pm - Addressing malnutrition collective responsibility: Sarwat Gillani Actress Sarwat Gillani said that addressing malnutrition was a collective responsibility. “It should be portrayed as everyone’s responsibility because only then can it be resolved because it is in every province,” Gillani said. “So we have to work on this problem collectively,” she added. 3:40pm - Sarwat Gillani stresses use of ‘intelligent marketing’ Actress Sarwat Gilani emphasised the use of “intelligent marketing” in addressing societal issues, including malnutrition. “Intelligent marketing is the answer to so many of our problems. In this day and age where everything is on a credit card or a mobile phone [..] if we have all the right creative minds along with experts, we can all sit down and come up with a strategic marketing campaign,” she said. 3:30pm - Film mogul highlights importance of radio, PTV in reaching the masses Satish Anand, the chairman of EverReady Pictures, highlighted the importance of radio and PTV for reaching the masses. He said that radio was widely listened to by people living in rural areas. He added that PTV could also be effectively used to communicate social issues. Satish Anand, the chairman of EverReady Pictures speaks at the conference. — White Star/ Tanveer Shahzad 3:20pm - Sarwat Gilani says malnutrition caused by host of factors Actress Sarwat Gilani, who is also an ambassador for Special Olympics Pakistan and the Indus Hospital and Health Network, said that there had been a lot of “repetition” during the conference as people cited data and statistics. “If this repetition, can be disseminated on an every day level, it would have a more lasting result,” she said. She said that malnutrition was not a “disease” and was caused by a host of factors. She also called for focusing on the solution rather than the problem. Actress Sarwat Gillani speaks at the conference. — White Star/ Tanveer Shahzad 3:17pm - Journalist notes lack of focus on nutrition in media Journalist Zarrar Khuhro termed malnutrition a “silent crisis” and went on to say that there was limited conversation about the issue in the media. “You will see a press release perhaps [..] but that does not cause a conversation at the household level and [..] if you can’t do that, then you have no hope of societal change”. “That is what we need, not just top-down change but critical mass at the family level, personal individual level, identifying this issue and seeking solutions and creating what we call a public buy-in,” he said. Journalist Zarrar Khuhro speaks at the conference, — White Star/ Tanveer Shahzad 3:12pm - Panel discussion on communicating for change begins A panel discussion on communicating for societal change has now begun. 3:10pm - Official says 1 in 4 children in Punjab suffering from stunted growth Dr Usman Ali Khan, the programme director of the Punjab Family Planning Programme, said that comparing the surveys from 2018 and 2024 showed progress. However, despite this improvement, there were 5.5m malnourished children in the province, he said. He said that one in four children in the province suffered from stunted growth. He said that the province was actively screening women and children that could be suffering from malnutrition and stunting. 3:05pm - Nutritional financing a provincial budgetary question, says Punjab govt official Punjab government’s special secretary, Aurangzaib Haider Khan, presented three priorities to the forum. “First, a common nutritional indicator so that provincial data can be compared, rather than merely collected,” Khan said. Secondly, he called for an “honest recognition of the fiscal architecture [under] the 18th Amendment” and added that nutritional financing was predominantly a provincial budgetary question. Third, Khan said was that “birth spacing also belongs inside the nutritional agenda, rather than besides it”. Punjab government’s special secretary, Aurangzaib Haider Khan, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/ Tanveer Shahzad 2:57pm - Govt official says Punjab carries majority of nutritional burden Punjab government’s special secretary, Aurangzaib Haider Khan, delivering his address, said that Punjab shouldered the majority of the country’s nutritional burden due to the size of its population “Let me be direct on what has moved in this scenario: Stunting among children under five has fallen from 36pc in 2018 to 27pc now.” However, the government official held that the progress made was insufficient, as “more than one in four children“ remain stunted, leading up to around 5.5m children across the province. 2:52pm - Minister says fathers must recognise a child’s nutrition as their responsibility Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said that public service messaging on nutrition must address the whole family, not just the mother. “Too often, we place the entire burden of a child’s nutrition on women, while decisions about food purchases, healthcare and women’s workloads may be taken by other members of the family. A mother cannot carry this responsibility alone,” he said. “Fathers must understand that nutrition is also their responsibility,” he said. 2:50pm - Minister calls for improving public service messaging Information Minister Attaullah Tarar highlighted the need for the right kind of messaging to tackle malnutrition. He said that communication could nutrition outcomes if it was done differently. “Public service messaging must move beyond telling people that malnutrition is a serious problem. Every message must give families practical steps they can take. Every message should have a result-oriented approach,” he said. He said that awareness programmes often focused on the problem rather than the solution. 2:44pm - Info minister says malnutrition not simply a health issues Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said that malnutrition was not simply a health issue. “It is a moral challenge, an economic imperative and a national emergency,” he said. The minister went on to say that malnutrition was shaped by maternal health, feeding practices, unsafe water, inadequate healthcare, climate vulnerabilities and unequal access to essential services. He further said that the Act for Nutrition conference should not be a one-off event, saying it should be an “action plan which we can implement throughout the year”. Information Minister Attaullah Tarar addresses the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 2:40pm - Info minister stresses need for communication, awareness to tackle malnutrition Information Minister Attaullah Tarar, in his address, said that communication and awareness were essential for tackling malnutrition. He hailed DawnMedia group for raising awareness of the issue. He said that more than 40pc of children in Pakistan were stunted, while maternal mortality rate was 155 deaths per 100,000 live births. “Malnutrition costs Pakistan more than $17bn annually. If the right kind of strategy can be deployed across the country, the impact it would have on our gross domestic growth would benefit the common man,” he said. “Behind every stunted child is potential that may never be fully realised. Behind every malnourished mother is a family at greater risk. And behind every year of inaction is another generation beginning life at a disadvantage,” he said. 2:00pm - Lunch break 1:40pm - UK expert stresses need for safely managed water and sanitation Oliver Cumming, the environmental health lead at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, said: “The prospect of safely managed water and sanitation in Pakistan is not something which can be achieved tomorrow, and it is not as simple as shifting gears that you go from basic to safely managed.” However, he suggested that recognition towards the goal could lead to universal access to safely managed WASH services sooner rather than later. “We have to be realistic that it will not happen tomorrow, but putting in place the investment, the political arguments […] universal access to safely managed services can become possible within a decade,” he added. “This is where we need to get if we really want to solve the problem of chronic malnutrition.” 1:25pm - Expert says water quality a ‘big issue’ for Pakistan Dr Saima Khan — a water, sanitation and hygiene policy specialist — called for targeting the 36 districts in the country contributing to stunting in children. She said that WASH infrastructure investments should be done in these districts. She also said that water quality was a “big issue” for Pakistan. She said that the country’s northern areas, Azad Jammu and Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan had no infrastructure for sanitation or sewerage. She said that this was deteriorating the quality of drinking water in these areas. 1:05pm - WB official calls for understanding WASH-related drivers of malnutrition Senior water specialist at the World Bank, Basharat Saeed, underscored the significance of gaining a “sophisticated understanding” of WASH-related drivers behind child malnutrition. “You need to look at what are the processes at a given location that are leading to the accumulation of faecal waste, accumulation in a way that it is exposing sensitive ecosystem and exposing people to faecal pathogens,” Saeed said. He added that it should also be made possible to track the common pathways for oral transmission for faecal material. “If you can map that out at the start of a programme design, then you know what sort of WASH investment is needed,” he said, stressing the need for a sophisticated understanding of WASH-related drivers of malnutrition. He added that as a result of adopting such an approach, the “proposed solution will also become slightly more comprehensive”. Senior water specialist at the World Bank, Basharat Saeed, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Muhammad Asim 12:49pm - UK expert says water and sanitation alone cannot end stunting Oliver Cumming, the environmental health lead at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, said that water and sanitation alone cannot end stunting, but it was essential part of the comprehensive strategies needed to address it. He said that for the water and sanitation sector, nutrition was often peripheral, adding that this needed to change. He said that 20pc of children in South Asia were stunted at birth, highlighting the need for prevention and an integrated approach to the issue. 12:45pm - WaterAid official calls for moving towards delivering multisectoral approach Country director at WaterAid, Mian Muhammad Junaid, stressed that the conversation on a multisectoral approach needed to move beyond talking and towards financing and delivering results. “We are working in silos; we still tend to organise ourselves in sectors, where nutrition sits in one policy sector, health in another, water and sanitation somewhere else, climate separately, social protection is another,” Junaid said. He went on to note that a child did not experience these boundaries; rather, it was a lived reality for them. “This is where I think Pakistan needs to move from talking about a multisectoral approach to actually financing and delivering one,” he added. 12:41pm - WaterAid official says child’s environment important for addressing malnutrition In his keynote speech, Mian Muhammad Junaid, the country director for WaterAid, raised alarm at the impact of lack of water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services on a child’s development and nutrition. “A child cannot be well nourished if the environment in which the child grows is making them sick,” he said. He said WASH services were often an “important but missed” aspect of addressing malnutrition. “WASH is a part of nutrition,“ Junaid said. “A child may receive the right food, nutritional counselling, cash transfer and access to health facilities, but if the child is repeatedly exposed to contaminated drinking water, faecal contamination, poor sanitation and an unhealthy environment, we are asking that child to grow and develop against very difficult odds,” he said. Mian Muhammad Junaid, the country director for WaterAid, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Muhammad Asim 12:40pm - Panel discussion on contribution of dirty water, poor sanitation to stunting begins A panel discussion on how dirty water and poor sanitation contribute to stunting has now begun. 12:38pm - BISP official says policies, legislation remain ‘only on paper’ Tehmina Gulzar, the deputy director of nutrition at the Benazir Income Support Programme, said that hygiene, agricultural, sanitation sectors had to come together to respond to malnutrition. She said that BISP had trained doctors, paramedical staff and teachers on adolescent nutrition to bring knowledge to communities. She also said that while policies and legislation were drafted, they were “only on paper”. “We need to bring them into practice. All sectors are working on [nutrition], but they are fragmented efforts,” she said, highlighting the need for the digital integration of all sectors. 12:31pm - Expert says malnutrition not ‘poverty-related’ Dr Farhana Memon, the programme director of Reproductive, Maternal, Neonatal and Child Health, dispelled the perception that malnutrition was tied to poverty. “It is said that malnutrition is just poverty-related; I don’t think so. I have been in the field for 27 years, and whenever I ask a woman what she has eaten for breakfast, she will tell me she had tea and rusk,” Dr Memon said. “We have failed to convince her that she can get an egg for the same cost,” she said. “Let’s take an example of two issues in public health — breastfeeding and micronutrient deficiencies — these are not poverty-related; it’s knowledge-related,” she said. 12:15pm - BISP official says social protection programmes can play ‘significant role’ in improving nutrition outcomes Tehmina Gulzar, the deputy director of nutrition at the Benazir Income Support Programme, said that social protection programmes can play a “significant role” in improving nutrition outcomes. She added that BISP was a very good example of how social protection programmes could contribute toward human capital development. She also said that BISP had a huge collection of data that could be used by different sectors involved in addressing nutrition. Tehmina Gulzar, the deputy director of nutrition at the Benazir Income Support Programme, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Muhammad Asim 12:01pm - Expert says nutrition cannot be viewed in isolation CEO of the Pakistan Alliance on Early Childhood Development Khadija Khan warned against viewing nutrition in isolation. “Because for holistic development, you need a complete package and that package is described in the nurturing care framework, which is talking about good health, adequate nutrition, responsive caregiving, safety, security and early learning opportunity.” She held that until and unless these inputs were met, it was not possible to achieve holistic child development. “We do talk about a multisectoral approach and an integrated approach, but still the families are knocking on different doors for different services. In reality, we do not really give integrated services to our children,” Khan added. 11:49am - Non-profit head says people do not ‘believe in the system’ Shahid Lone, the chairman of the Allah Walay Foundation, said that if policymakers and those responsible for implementation did not put their “soul” into what they were doing, then what they were aiming for “would never work”. He acknowledged that his take was more “philosophical”. He highlighted that government officials say one thing on stage and another when they are behind the scenes. “We have policies, we have departments, but we have people who do not believe in the system,” he said. He questioned how those who did not have vision or believed in their work could implement policies. Shahid Lone, the chairman of the Allah Walay Foundation, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Muhammad Asim 11:37am - ‘Behaviour of healthcare providers pathetic’ Dr Farhana Memon, the programme director of Reproductive, Maternal, Neonatal and Child Health, also criticised the behaviour of healthcare workers. “The behaviour of healthcare providers is pathetic,” Dr Memon said, noting that most healthcare workers did not counsel patients on family planning, nutrition, or vaccination. “We have been trying to change the behaviour of the community for the past decade, but now it is time to change the behaviour of healthcare providers.” “If a person or a woman comes into contact with you, please don’t waste the opportunity,” she urged. 11:34am - Expert decries lack of dedicated funding for nutrition Programme director of Reproductive, Maternal, Neonatal, and Child Health Dr Farhana Memon decried the lack of funds to address malnutrition. “If you want to [translate] policies into action, you should have some cost,” she said, adding that donors largely funded efforts to end malnutrition. “This is not the solution,” Memon remarked, adding that nutrition should be treated as a separate entity. She further urged that the government must utilise every access point as an opportunity to counsel families about nutrition. Programme director of Reproductive, Maternal, Neonatal, and Child Health Dr Farhana Memon speaks at the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Muhammad Asim 11:25am - Session on multisectoral approach to nutrition begins A session on the multisectoral approach to nutrition has now begun. 11:20am - KP CM says govt working on addressing malnutrition Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, in a video message, said that facilitation centres were being established to address malnutrition among pregnant women and young children. He said that the provincial government, under PTI founder Imran Khan’s vision, was working on this issue and others. He ended by thanking DawnMedia for highlighting malnutrition and other social issues. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi’s video message at the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 11:10am - Govt official calls for cohesive national narrative on malnutrition Dr Shabana Haider, member (population) in the Planning Commission of Pakistan, stressed the need for a cohesive national narrative in addressing malnutrition. “Do not go switching your national narrative; sometimes it is said that two kids are enough, sometimes it is one, and sometimes you ask women to time their pregnancies. Please develop a narrative that you can lead on and that everybody — from development partners to private sector — can converge on,” she said. 11:00am - Govt official says nutritional challenges cannot be addressed without acknowledging population dynamics Dr Shabana Haider, member (population) in the Planning Commission of Pakistan, said that nutritional challenges could not be addressed without acknowledging population dynamics and demographic dividends could not be reaped without investing in nutrition. She said that while Pakistan had done a lot on the policy side, the documents themselves were not enough. “We are very good at framing policies … sorry, excuse me, this has to change … let’s all recognise that our priority has not been population,” she said, adding that population had been neglected as a subject. 10:50am - KP govt official says malnutrition, family planning interlinked Dr Fazal Majeed, the director of nutrition at the Directorate General Health Services for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, said that Pakistan had a stunting growth rate of 40pc, adding that it was 48pc in KP’s merged districts. He also said that almost 40pc of women of reproductive age were also anaemic, calling the figures “alarming”. “Malnutrition, family planning … are interlinked,” he said. He said some of the barriers in KP were fragmented delivery points, geographical and security-related. Dr Fazal Majeed, the director of nutrition at the Directorate General Health Services for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference, — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 10:35am - Public health professional says history of Pakistan’s health programmes ‘one of isolation’ Dr Talib Lashari, a public health professional with the Sindh government’s health department, said that the nexus between nutrition and family planning was “well established but poorly practised in Pakistan”. “The history of Pakistan’s public health programmes and initiatives is one of isolation. All the programmes have been well-designed and, to some extent, properly funded, but they were implemented in isolation,” he said. 10:24am - Govt adviser says nutrition needs to be reclassified as a capital expenditure Adnan Pasha Siddiqui, the adviser to the minister of finance, said that nutrition needed to be reclassified as a capital expenditure rather than as an expense. “So this single accounting decision suppresses the investment narrative permanently … these are fundamental flaws we need to correct,” he said. Adnan Pasha Siddiqui, the adviser to the minister of finance, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 10:17am - Govt adviser says lack of investment in nutrition hurts Pakistan’s GDP Adnan Pasha Siddiqui, the adviser to the minister of finance, said that burgeoning population and lack of resources were a “collective failure of capital investment”. “We are reflecting everything nutrition-related as a health expenditure … every rupee that is withheld from a pregnant women’s diet is a deduction from the country’s gross domestic product in the future,” he said. He said that in the country, nutrition was divided across several sectors. Siddiqui said that the annual loss from malnutrition was $17bn. He said that in South Asia, labour productivity was suppressed because of nutrition. “And it is a structural liability to our sovereign credit profile,” he said. 10:08am - World Bank official says nutrition is viewed through ‘a human capital lens’ Sara Shahzad, the senior health specialist from the World Bank, said that the group had 10-year country partnership framework with the government of Pakistan focused on six priority areas, one of which was stunting reduction. “So the way the World Bank looks at population stabilisation and nutrition, specifically the stunting agenda, is through a human capital lens,” she said. Talking about stunting, she said that 30-40pc of it occurred before a child was born. “So, the first 1,000 days are absolutely critical but also the adolescence period,” she said. Sara Shahzad, the senior health specialist from the World Bank, speaks at the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 9:58am - Expert highlights ‘experimentation’ in Pakistan’s population planning Dr Ali Mir, the country director for the Population Council, said that there was always a tendency in Pakistan of “making the same mistakes again and again”. Talking about Pakistan’s previous population reforms, he highlighted wavering political commitment and policy inconsistency. “We never explicitly had a population policy till 2002. It was always couched in development planning,” he said. He said that due to this, Pakistan was constantly “experimenting”. Dr Mir said that now things were moving in the right direction, with the establishment of the Population Council. Dr Ali Mir, the country director for the Population Council, speaks at the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 9:55am - Doctor says nutrition is ‘not an isolated event’ Dr Saima Hamid, the programme and research lead at the Population Council, said that Pakistan’s population growth rate is at 2.55pc. She said that in 28 years, the country’s population would double, putting a huge burden on resources. “This clearly is a challenge of not just the quantity but also the quality of diet. We need to ensure that diverse nutrition reaches those most vulnerable,” she said. She also said that Pakistan’s domestic food security was on the decline, adding that “nutrition is not just an isolated event”. “One sector isn’t really responsible … there is a clear intersection of nutrition, food security, health, purchasing power,” she said. 9:52am - Session on population and resources has begun A session on how a nation cannot feed, educate or employ what it cannot count on sustaining has now begun. 9:50am - 2nd day of conference begins The second day of the conference begins with a short film titled Leaky Guts from the Aga Khan University.

items.title: The coup doesn’t need soldiers anymore: Social media and the new assault on African democracy
items.description: In an earlier piece for this column, I wrote about Ananse the trickster who built webs not to trap flies but to acquire stories, and with them, control over what the world came to believe. I argued the platforms shaping African minds today play Ananse’s game at a planetary scale and that Africa still had not written the philosophy to govern the web it inherited. That piece was about the missing foundation. This one is about what is already collapsing on top of it: social media is no longer simply changing how Africans talk to one another. It is quietly reshaping the conditions under which they decide who governs them. The Coup Has Changed Its Uniform For most of the second half of the twentieth century, the fastest route to capturing an African state ran through the barracks soldiers, a seized radio station, a communiqué read out before dawn. Whole generations here learned to recognise the sound of a coup before they understood the politics behind it. Sometimes the barracks had help from outside. The 2011 NATO campaign that ended with Muammar Gaddafi’s killing was built, a 2016 UK Parliament inquiry found, on intelligence presented with “unjustified certainty” about a threat to civilians in Benghazi. Five years on, Barack Obama, who ordered US involvement, called failing to plan for what followed “the worst mistake” of his presidency. Libya has not recovered since proof, well before any algorithm existed, that a state can be dismantled on the strength of a story that turns out not to be true. The old lever was still being pulled, too. Mali in 2020. Guinea and Burkina Faso in 2021 and 2022. Niger in 2023 coups in the fullest, oldest sense, driven by insurgency, elite fracture, and state weakness, not by a hashtag. The African Union suspended all four. Rather than wait to be readmitted, three Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger broke away entirely, forming their own Alliance of Sahel States and walking out of ECOWAS in January 2025, framing it as resistance to institutions they no longer trusted. And now the continent is discovering the barracks were never the only door in. One of the most efficient ways to destabilise a nation today needs no soldier, a smartphone, a grievance, and an algorithm hungry enough to reward whichever one spreads fastest, because attention curdles into perception, perception into trust, and trust is the raw material legitimacy is built from. In Ethiopia, internal documents released through the “Facebook Papers” showed the company had flagged the country as high-risk years before its civil war broke out and still failed to contain hate speech that researchers later linked to real ethnic violence. In Kenya’s 2017 election, an executive of Cambridge Analytica, the firm behind its microtargeting, was filmed describing how his company “put information into the bloodstream of the internet” of a nation still carrying the memory of the 2007–08 post-election killings. Different eras, different tools. The same outcome: outrage travels faster than correction, and the correction arrives to a public that has already moved on. Interest Has No Party and No Passport Social media does not optimise for truth. It optimises for whatever holds attention, and attention, we now know with painful clarity, is held longest by fear, tribal loyalty, and righteous anger. This is not a Ghanaian problem, a Kenyan problem, or an Ethiopian problem. It is a design problem that behaves identically regardless of which political party benefits from it this week and regardless of which country the loudest voice happens to be broadcasting from. None of this makes the algorithm a villain by design. The same feeds broke information monopolies that had protected entrenched power for decades: Sudan’s 2019 uprising, Nigeria’s #EndSARS, Ghana’s own #FixTheCountry all ran through them too. The mechanism is neutral; only the outcome tells you which side it served this time. Burkina Faso shows both sides of this inside one country. The same algorithmic machinery that tears a state down elsewhere is, there, also being used to manufacture one man’s legitimacy: the Africa Center for Strategic Studies has traced a coordinated, AI-driven campaign of deepfakes and bot networks, orchestrated by President Ibrahim Traoré’s own brothers, who run the junta’s digital economy and communications portfolios to inflate his image across the continent, running alongside genuine reforms and a genuine crackdown on the press covering them. The recommender system that rewards outrage is a decade old; what generative AI adds is sharper still synthetic video and cloned voices convincing enough to have a chief, an imam, or a president appear to say something he never said. The algorithm does not care whether it is used to bring a government down or prop one up. It only rewards whichever version performs. That is precisely why our current approach to accountability keeps failing: incitement is forgivable the moment it wears a party colour, and untouchable the moment it is posted from beyond our borders. A public figure who threatens through political language, or a diaspora voice stirring unrest at home, should not be exempt because of who they support or where they post from. That standard has to be written narrowly, aimed at inciting a specific, provable act and not at diaspora political voice itself, which African governments have too often relabelled “outside interference” to silence dissent. Africa needs a policy that judges the act on its own terms, not one borrowed from Silicon Valley, not one that bends on affiliation, fame, or address. Why the Engineers Cannot Fix This Alone Every proposed solution so far has come from the technology sector itself: better moderation, better classifiers, better fact-checking. These matter, but share a blind spot: built for platform metrics, not community trust. A chief in a Northern Ghanaian community will recognise the phrase that could ignite a chieftaincy dispute faster than any keyword filter trained in San Francisco ever will. A council of elders knows which rumour is a joke and which one is a match dropped near dry grass. This is why the argument I made about AI governance needing a philosophical anchor applies just as urgently here: platform governance in Africa cannot be left to technologists and legislators alone. It needs traditional leaders, religious authorities, and community elders in the room, alongside policymakers genuinely rooted in the cultures they govern, not merely fluent in Silicon Valley’s vocabulary and platform representatives themselves. None of them belongs there as a ceremonial guest, brought in only to critique what the algorithm already got wrong: each needs real authority to define what it should look like for African communities in the first place and to catch incitement before it spreads rather than after. Every seat at that table, elders included, carries the same discipline fixed terms, a plural bench rather than one voice, and an appeals path outside its own authority. The 2020 documentary The Social Dilemma unsettled global audiences by showing, through the engineers who built these systems, that outrage was not a side effect of engagement optimisation it was the point. Africa does not need a documentary to discover this; we are living the unfiltered version, without the luxury of watching from a safe distance. “The old coup announced itself with tanks in the street. This one announces itself as a trending topic, and by the time we recognise it, the trust it has burned is already gone.” Retrieving What We Already Have There is a reason Akan tradition gave us Sankofa the wisdom of turning back to retrieve what has been left behind before continuing forward. Sankofa does not promise our ancestors anticipated algorithms; it promises that principles built for one era can be retrieved and translated for another. The same communal accountability that once made an elder’s rebuke carry more weight than any court summons can still apply to a village square that never sleeps and reaches a million people before breakfast. Africa spent the twentieth century learning, at a devastating cost, how to recognise a coup. It cannot afford to spend the twenty-first learning day at the same cost on how to recognise this one. The room this requires elders and engineers, chiefs and coders, policymakers and platforms is not one we convene at our convenience. The window is closing now. Not tomorrow.

items.title: JM 2026 : l’Algérie termine dans le top 10 portée par le triplé de Kaylia Nemour
items.description: Le rideau est tombé sur les Jeux méditerranéens de Tarente 2026 en Italie ce jeudi 3 septembre. L’Algérie a terminé à la 9ᵉ place avec un total de 40 médailles dont 13 en or. L’Italie (66 médailles d’or, 1ᵉʳ), la Turquie (41 médailles d’or, 2ᵉ) et la Grèce (26 médailles d’or, 3ᵉ) occupent les trois premières places. La France, qui n’a pas participé avec ses meilleures athlètes, comme de nombreux pays européens qui ont donné la chance aux plus jeunes de s’affirmer, a fini à la 4ᵉ place, devant l’Égypte, l’Espagne, le Maroc et le Portugal. Kaylia Nemour décroche 3 médailles d’or Pour l’Algérie, elle a réalisé la « meilleure performance » de l'histoire des Jeux méditerranéens organisés hors du pays, et la deuxième meilleure participation jamais enregistrée après Oran 2022, s’est félicité le Comité olympique et sportif algérien, qui a félicité les athlètes qui ont fait flotter le drapeau national à Tarente. Et si l’Algérie a pu engranger 13 médailles d’or, c’est en partie grâce à la gymnaste Kaylia Nemour qui a décroché l’or à trois reprises. La championne olympique algérienne a étoffé son palmarès avec une médaille de bronze dans le concours par équipes. C’est elle qui a permis à l’Algérie de remonter au classement et de finir dans le Top 10, après un début poussif. L’article JM 2026 : l’Algérie termine dans le top 10 portée par le triplé de Kaylia Nemour est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: 6 JI workers arrested for allegedly burning motorcyles, tyres to obstruct traffic at Karachi's Korangi Crossing
items.description: KARACHI: Six workers of the Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) were arrested in Karachi on Wednesday on the accusation of setting motorcycles and tyres on fire at Korangi Crossing to block the roads, police said. The development coincided with JI’s nationwide strike against the petroleum levy, which the party said was being observed in a peaceful manner. In a statement, the party also seemed to distance itself from the burning of the two-wheelers and tyres, alleging that the government was resorting to “cheap tactics” to suppress its protest. Without naming anyone, the JI said “miscreants” were responsible for the Korangi Crossing incident. Videos — said to be of the incident — were circulating on social media and showed burned remnants of two motorcycles, alongside burning tyres laid out in a row to obstruct a road. Cars and motorcycles, however, were seen continuing to drive around the burning tyres to cross the obstruction. Korangi Senior Superintendent of Police Hussain Janwari said while speaking to Dawn that law enforcers had arrested six JI workers in connection with the incident. According to him, the arrested party workers got two old motorcycles and some tyres from a junk dealer and “are said to have set them on fire at Korangi Crossing to block the traffic”. He said police “controlled the situation” after reaching the site. A first information report has been registered against the six suspects under the anti-terror law, he added. Earlier, a statement issued by the Chief Minister’s Office said Sindh CM Murad Ali Shah had taken notice of “unidentified people creating a law and order situation” in Korangi. He directed that the matter be investigated immediately and “action be taken against miscreants without any discrimination”, the statement said. “Individuals involved in setting motorcycles on fire at Korangi Crossing should be immediately arrested,” the statement quoted the CM as saying. He also sought a report from the Sindh police chief on the incident, adding that “miscreants will not be allowed to destroy peace in the city”. Meanwhile, the JI noted the arrest of its workers in Korangi in a statement and demanded their immediate release. The party claimed that the traders were supporting their “struggle” and the government was trying to suppress the protest.

items.title: Désinformation en période de crise : Le CSC entre pédagogie, veille et sanctions
items.description: Le Conseil supérieur de la communication (CSC) a exposé son dispositif pour contenir les dérives informationnelles en période de crise. Formation des professionnels, sensibilisation du public, monitoring des médias et sanctions ; l'institution mise sur une régulation à plusieurs niveaux. Objectif, faire face à la désinformation et aux discours de haine qui gagnent l'espace médiatique burkinabè. C'est dans ce contexte qu'Abdoulaye Dao, directeur général de la publicité et de l'observation des contenus du CSC, a présenté le rôle de l'instance de régulation dans la gestion de l'information en période de crise. C'était au cours d'un atelier tenu du 27 au 29 juillet 2026 à Koudougou. Dans une salle attentive, les journalistes et web-activistes prennent des notes. La question n'est pas seulement de savoir comment produire et diffuser une information en période de crise, mais aussi de comprendre jusqu'où va la responsabilité de ceux qui la mettent en circulation. Intitulé « Rôle et responsabilité du Conseil supérieur de la communication dans la régulation de l'information en période de crise », l'exposé du directeur général de la publicité et de l'observation des contenus du CSC, Abdoulaye Dao, met en lumière une stratégie articulée autour de deux leviers. Ceux de prévenir les dérives en amont et intervenir lorsqu'elles surviennent. Créé en 1995, le CSC est une autorité administrative indépendante chargée de réguler la communication au public et de promouvoir la liberté d'expression et de presse au Burkina Faso. Son champ de compétence s'est progressivement élargi. Initialement centré sur l'information, il couvre désormais un domaine plus vaste de la communication, notamment la publicité. Depuis fin 2023, une nouvelle étape est franchie. Avec l'adoption de la loi organique n°041-2023/ALT du 21 novembre 2023, le champ de régulation du CSC s'étend également aux médias numériques, notamment aux réseaux sociaux. Une évolution que l'institution justifie par les mutations rapides des technologies de l'information et de la communication et par la montée de la désinformation et des discours de haine. Le changement de paradigme est considérable. Avec le Web 2.0, chacun peut désormais produire, commenter et relayer de l'information. Le nombre de producteurs de contenus explose, tandis que les frontières entre professionnels et non-professionnels deviennent plus poreuses. Dans un contexte marqué par la crise sécuritaire, cette multiplication des voix peut aussi amplifier les contenus trompeurs, haineux ou préjudiciables. Pour le CSC, il ne suffit donc plus d'intervenir lorsque le mal est fait. La régulation commence en amont. Prévenir avant de sanctionner Abdoulaye Dao insiste d'abord sur la dimension pédagogique du travail du régulateur. La liberté d'expression, rappelle-t-il, doit aller de pair avec le droit du public à une information de qualité, respectueuse de la loi, de l'éthique et de la déontologie. Cette mission conduit le CSC à multiplier les actions de formation auprès des professionnels des médias. Car si plusieurs instituts assurent la formation initiale aux métiers de l'information, le perfectionnement demeure indispensable. Le régulateur organise ainsi des sessions de formation continue destinées aux différents maillons de la chaîne de production et de diffusion de l'information. Les participants y sont notamment invités à revisiter les textes qui encadrent le secteur de la communication, les règles d'éthique et de déontologie, les bonnes pratiques liées aux émissions d'expression directe ou encore les techniques de vérification des faits. Le fact-checking occupe ainsi une place importante dans cette démarche. Dans un environnement où une information peut être produite, partagée et devenir virale en quelques minutes, vérifier avant de publier ou de relayer devient une exigence professionnelle. Mais le CSC ne limite pas son action aux seuls journalistes. Sensibiliser ceux qui produisent et ceux qui partagent Sur les réseaux sociaux, la diffusion de l'information dépasse largement le cercle des professionnels. Influenceurs, administrateurs de pages, créateurs de contenus et simples utilisateurs peuvent tous contribuer à faire circuler une information. D'où la nécessité, selon le régulateur, d'agir également auprès des non-professionnels et du public. Le constat dressé par Abdoulaye Dao est sans détour. Plusieurs manquements relevés par le CSC seraient liés à une méconnaissance des règles. La sensibilisation apparaît donc comme un moyen de réduire les dérives avant qu'elles ne deviennent des infractions. L'institution multiplie à cet effet les initiatives. Elle plaide pour l'adaptation des textes aux défis de la convergence numérique et au contexte socio-sécuritaire. Elle participe également à l'élaboration de référentiels destinés à favoriser un usage responsable des médias, particulièrement des réseaux sociaux. Parmi ces outils figurent notamment les « dix Conseils du CSC sur l'usage des réseaux sociaux », les sept points d'attention destinés aux journalistes et aux patrons de médias, ainsi que des guides et chartes encadrant les émissions et médias à caractère confessionnel. Le travail de proximité complète ce dispositif. Des tournées de sensibilisation sont organisées dans plusieurs chefs-lieux de région pour expliquer aux populations, notamment aux jeunes, les conséquences de la désinformation et des discours de haine. Des conférences publiques consacrées au bon usage des réseaux sociaux sont également initiées. Le CSC cherche par ailleurs à renforcer le dialogue entre journalistes et forces de défense et de sécurité. Des ateliers de réflexion sont consacrés à cette collaboration, avec un objectif de faciliter l'accès aux sources et améliorer le traitement de l'information sécuritaire. Des microprogrammes diffusés dans les médias viennent enfin renforcer cette politique d'éducation aux médias. Mais malgré cet arsenal préventif, certaines dérives persistent. Le régulateur doit alors changer de posture. 500 médias professionnels à réguler Le CSC dispose également de moyens d'action à l'encontre des auteurs de manquements. Pour savoir où intervenir, encore faut-il observer l'espace médiatique. C'est le rôle du monitoring. Le paysage médiatique burkinabè compte aujourd'hui environ 500 médias professionnels, toutes catégories confondues. À ce volume s'ajoutent désormais certains médias sociaux non professionnels entrant dans le champ de régulation, notamment ceux disposant d'au moins 5 000 abonnés ou followers. La tâche du régulateur devient alors particulièrement vaste. Pour y répondre, le CSC s'appuie sur un Centre de monitoring et sur un dispositif technique capable d'enregistrer et de stocker les productions audiovisuelles diffusées sur le territoire national. Un service spécifique assure également le suivi de la presse écrite, de la presse en ligne et des réseaux sociaux. Le dispositif repose aussi sur une déconcentration des services. Des délégations régionales sont implantées à Bobo-Dioulasso, Fada N'Gourma et Ouahigouya, tandis que des représentants provinciaux contribuent au suivi des contenus. Cette veille permet au CSC de disposer de données sur les manquements constatés et, lorsque cela est nécessaire, d'enclencher la procédure de sanction. De l'avertissement à l'interdiction La loi organique n°041-2023/ALT du 21 novembre 2023 prévoit plusieurs niveaux de sanctions à l'encontre des personnes morales responsables de manquements. La mise en demeure peut constituer une première réponse. Viennent ensuite, selon la gravité des faits, la suspension temporaire, la réduction de la durée de l'autorisation pour l'audiovisuel, l'amende ou encore l'interdiction définitive. Une nouveauté importante concerne également les personnes physiques. Le CSC peut désormais prononcer à leur encontre certaines mesures, notamment l'avertissement ou la suspension de toute activité de communication médiatique. Pour les professionnels, l'institution peut aussi demander le retrait temporaire ou définitif de la carte de presse. Le champ d'intervention du régulateur ne s'arrête pas là. Lorsque des contenus audiovisuels sont jugés illicites ou malveillants, le CSC peut demander le déréférencement des adresses électroniques donnant accès à certains services audiovisuels en ligne. Il peut également, sur saisine des titulaires de droits, demander aux fournisseurs d'accès à internet de restreindre l'accès à des contenus audiovisuels exploités illégalement. L'institution a déjà fait usage de ces prérogatives. En 2024, plusieurs sites web dont BBC, RFI, Human Rights Watch et France 24, ont ainsi fait l'objet de mesures de suspension d'accès à la suite de manquements constatés par le régulateur. Des responsables de pages Facebook et TikTok ont également été auditionnés ou interpellés. Une responsabilité qui dépasse le seul CSC À travers ce dispositif, le Conseil supérieur de la communication entend jouer pleinement son rôle dans la protection de l'espace public médiatique. Mais le directeur général de la publicité et de l'observation des contenus du CSC le reconnaît. Malgré les actions de prévention et les mesures dissuasives, Abdoulaye Dao souligne que la désinformation et les discours de haine restent préoccupants. La réponse ne peut donc reposer sur le seul régulateur. Dans un contexte de crise, où une information mal vérifiée peut alimenter la peur, la confusion ou les tensions, il estime que la responsabilité est collective. Elle concerne les journalistes, les patrons de médias, les créateurs de contenus, les utilisateurs des réseaux sociaux, mais aussi les différentes structures publiques et les organisations de la société civile. En somme, pour le CSC, la régulation ne consiste pas seulement à sanctionner les mauvaises pratiques. Elle commence par l'éducation, la prévention et la responsabilisation. Car face à un phénomène aussi mouvant que la désinformation, l'enjeu n'est peut-être pas de prétendre faire disparaître le fléau, mais de construire collectivement, un espace public suffisamment responsable et résilient pour en limiter les effets. Lire aussi : Burkina/Cybercriminalité : Les bons réflexes pour renforcer sa sécurité numérique Hamed Nanéma Lefaso.net

items.title: How to apply: Nigerian Air Force begins recruitment exercise

items.title: Works and Housing Minister pushes to cut Kaneshie road closure from one year to 6–9 months
items.description: Works and Housing Minister Ahmed Ibrahim has called for a review of the proposed one-year closure of a section of the Winneba–Accra road at Kaneshie. He warned that the planned engineering works could cause severe disruption to commuters, businesses and traffic flow if the closure is not carefully coordinated. The Minister made the remarks during an inspection of the project site ahead of the temporary closure of about 1.5 kilometres of the road, from the Kaneshie Roundabout to Accra Academy. The closure is expected to begin next week to allow contractors to undertake critical engineering works on the stretch. While acknowledging the importance of the project, Mr Ibrahim said its potential impact must be fully assessed before work begins. He stressed that the decision required coordination among several government institutions rather than being left to a single ministry. “I’m not the Minister for Roads, I’m not the Finance Minister, and I’m not the National Security Minister. All these ministers need to be convinced and understand the effect of what is going to happen here,” he said. The Minister warned that shutting down one of Accra’s busiest road corridors for 12 months could result in significant congestion and inconvenience for thousands of motorists who rely on the route daily. “If we start, there will be a lot of inconvenience. The situation will be chaotic,” he added. Mr Ibrahim urged the Ministry of Roads and Highways, Finance Ministry, National Security Ministry and the Greater Accra Regional Coordinating Council to work together on measures to minimise the impact of the closure. He said adequate arrangements must be put in place before contractors move to site to prevent the closure from worsening congestion in the capital. The Minister also questioned the proposed 12-month completion period, suggesting that the timeline should be reviewed and, if possible, reduced. He proposed a completion period of between six and nine months as a possible alternative. The planned engineering works are intended to improve the condition of the Kaneshie section of the Winneba–Accra road. However, authorities have yet to announce detailed traffic diversion arrangements ahead of the planned closure, leaving commuters and businesses awaiting clarity on how traffic will be managed during the construction period.

items.title: Yaoundé : l’Hôpital Central célèbre la kinésithérapie et la lutte contre les AVC
items.description: © DR Du 1er au 8 septembre 2026, l'Hôpital Central de Yaoundé organise une semaine dédiée à la kinésithérapie avec bilans gratuits et symposium sur les maladies cardiovasculaires et les AVC, pour promouvoir l'accès aux soins et la rééducation fonctionnelle. Depuis le 1er septembre 2026, l'Hôpital Central de Yaoundé célèbre la kinésithérapie à travers une série d'activités sanitaires et scientifiques qui se poursuivent jusqu'au 8 septembre prochain. Jusqu'au 7 septembre, l'établissement propose aux populations des bilans et prises en charge kinésithérapiques gratuits. Une initiative forte dans un contexte où l'accès aux soins de rééducation reste un défi pour de nombreux Camerounais. Selon Élysée Mvondo, Major du Service de Physio-Kinésithérapie, cette campagne vise à faciliter l'accès aux soins, à sensibiliser sur l'importance de la rééducation et à mettre en lumière le rôle essentiel des kinésithérapeutes dans la récupération fonctionnelle et l'autonomie des patients, notamment après un accident vasculaire cérébral (AVC). Le point d'orgue est prévu le 8 septembre, à l'occasion de la Journée internationale de la kinésithérapie. Un symposium consacré aux « maladies cardiovasculaires et aux AVC » clôturera la semaine. Ce rendez-vous scientifique réunit médecins, kinésithérapeutes et infirmiers autour de la prévention, de la prise en charge et de la rééducation de ces pathologies, première cause de handicap acquis. À travers cette mobilisation, l'Hôpital Central de Yaoundé réaffirme son engagement en faveur de soins accessibles et de qualité, conformément à sa devise : « Service – Qualité – Probité ». Cet article Yaoundé : l'Hôpital Central célèbre la kinésithérapie et la lutte contre les AVC est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

Il s’agit de Gaynako, Diabong-Corp et Kaaraange Kids. Elles ont été désignées à l’issue d’un exercice de présentation composé de plusieurs acteurs de référence de l’écosystème entrepreneurial et de l’innovation qui avait réuni 20 startups présélectionnées. À l’issue du Pitch national organisé par le ministère des Télécommunications et du Numérique, à travers la Commission d'évaluation, d'appui et de coordination (CEAC), trois startups ont été sélectionnées pour représenter le Sénégal à la 2ᵉ édition des ECOWAS Startup Awards, prévue à Abuja, au Nigéria, du 28 au 30 septembre 2026. « Réunissant 20 startups présélectionnées, le Pitch National a donné lieu à un exercice de présentation devant un jury composé de plusieurs acteurs de référence de l’écosystème entrepreneurial et de l’innovation, parmi lesquels Abdou Mbacké Lo, Head of Innovation and Startup Support de l’Adepme, en qualité de membre du jury », indique l'Agence de développement et d’encadrement des petites et moyennes entreprises (Adepme). A lire aussi : Compétitivité des entreprises : l’Adepme et la Direction des PME renforcent leurs synergies Ainsi, à l’issue de cette sélection, Gaynako, une société de conseil en marketing digital ; Diabong-Corp, spécialisée dans l’usinage à commande numérique ; et Kaaraange Kids, une solution digitale qui permet aux enfants d'alerter leurs parents en cas de danger et aux parents d'être toujours au courant de leur position, de leur état de santé physique et mentale ; porteront les couleurs du Sénégal lors de cette prochaine édition. Leur sélection vient mettre en lumière, selon l’Agence sénégalaise en charge de l’encadrement des PME, la diversité des solutions développées par les startups nationales et leur capacité à se positionner sur des espaces de compétition et de visibilité à l’échelle régionale.
