Plus d'une trentaine de participants prennent part a cette session d'un mois, organisee a Yorosso et Kiffosso. La formation porte notamment sur les methodes de preparation et de conduite des lecons. Selon le Centre d'Animation Pedagogique de Yorosso, cette initiative devrait contribuer a reduire le manque d'enseignants dans certains villages du cercle. L’article Yorosso : des jeunes diplômés formés au métier d’enseignant est apparu en premier sur Studio Tamani - Informations, débats, magazines : toute l’actualité du Mali, en 5 langues .

items.title: CSSPS explains how raw scores can override aggregate in SHS placement
items.description: The Coordinator of the Computerised School Selection and Placement System (CSSPS), Sherif Sulemana, has explained how candidates are ranked and matched with their preferred senior high schools, programmes and residential options during the placement process. Speaking on the Joy FM Super Morning Show on Thursday, September 3, Mr Sulemana said the process starts with ranking candidates by aggregate score before their school and programme choices are considered. “So the placement process is quite simple and straightforward. First of all, we rank candidates based on their aggregate scores,” he explained. He said candidates are ranked from the best aggregate of six to the lowest aggregate of 54. “If you have about 620,000 candidates, we rank them from the top, which is the six, to the bottom, which is an aggregate of 54,” he said. After ranking the candidates, the CSSPS considers the choices they made when selecting schools. These include the particular senior high school they want to attend, the programme they want to study, and whether they prefer day or boarding. Mr Sulemana explained that a candidate could, for instance, choose Tamale Senior High School, select General Science and indicate a preference for boarding. The system then considers whether the candidate’s aggregate score is strong enough to secure a place based on the available slots for that school, programme and residential status. “So we match the candidates’ aggregate scores to their choices, to their schools, and to the programmes and the residence of study they want,” he said. Mr Sulemana said the raw scores become important when candidates have the same aggregate score and are competing for the same limited space. He gave the example of two candidates who both obtain an aggregate of six and choose Tamale Senior High School, General Science and boarding. In that situation, the system needs another basis to determine which candidate gets the available place. “That’s where we use the raw scores to break the tie between the candidates,” he explained. According to him, the aggregate score remains the main basis for ranking candidates, while raw scores are used to separate candidates who are tied. “We can compute, but once we are using the aggregate scores, we only bring in the raw scores to break a tie,” he said. Mr Sulemana also explained a less obvious aspect of the placement system, where a candidate with a higher aggregate number could secure a place ahead of another candidate with a lower aggregate. He said this can happen when the candidates are competing for the same school, programme and residential option and their raw scores are considered. The explanation is linked to how grades are determined under the current grading system. Mr Sulemana said that a candidate could score 60 in a subject and obtain a grade one if that was the highest performance in that subject. In another subject, however, a candidate could score 90 but receive a lower grade if other candidates performed better. “So if someone had scored 90 and gotten, say, a two, and someone scores 60 and gets a one, that means the 90 is higher than the 60,” he said. He said this is why raw scores can sometimes provide a better indication of a candidate’s actual performance when candidates are competing for the same place. “That’s where sometimes we rely on the raw scores so that the raw scores now become the true reflection of the candidate, not the aggregate score,” he explained. He gave an example of two candidates competing for the same place, with one having an aggregate six and the other an aggregate eight. “So based on that as well, you can have a candidate with an aggregate six, another with an aggregate eight, competing for the same slot in the same school, the same programme, and the same residential status, and the one with the eight goes in because he has a higher raw score than the one with the six,” he said. The explanation has also highlighted the need for candidates and parents to better understand how raw scores are used in the placement process. Mr Sulemana admitted that the CSSPS may need to do more to educate the public about the system. “I also concede that maybe we have to go beyond just the aggregate scores and educate the general public on using the raw scores in the placement process as well,” he said. He also acknowledged concerns about the grading system and said the CSSPS had previously considered whether it should be reviewed. “During our initial engagements on the placements, I mean, we conceded that we may have to take a second look at using the state line system for the grading,” he said. He explained that the current system can produce situations where raw scores vary significantly even when candidates receive similar or better grades. Mr Sulemana also assured candidates and parents that the placement exercise was ready for release. When asked whether the process had been completed, he said the team was putting final touches to the system ahead of the expected release on Friday, September 4. “We are set. That assurance we can give the general public. We are set. There’s no cause for alarm. We are set,” he said.

items.title: Real Madrid open disciplinary proceedings against Asencio
items.description: Real Madrid have opened disciplinary proceedings against defender Raul Asencio, who was last month convicted of drink-driving, coach Jose Mourinho said on Thursday. The 23-year-old centre-back was more than three times over the legal limit during the August 16 incident. Asencio was convicted in a trial held in San Bartolome de Tirajana, a village in Gran Canaria, and fined 14,400 euros ($16,700), while his driving licence was suspended for eight months, a court source told AFP on Wednesday. This week, Asencio is due to face another court case in Gran Canaria, involving the alleged non-consensual sharing of a sexual video dating back to 2023. “He’s a model professional. When he was fit, no one trained as hard as him,” Mourinho told reporters. “Now that he’s been injured for a few weeks, he’s the first to arrive and the last to leave (training). “But a Real Madrid player remains so 24 hours a day, seven days a week, 12 months a year. “Everything you do outside the pitch represents Real Madrid and could affect the club’s prestige. “I’m not happy. Everyone makes mistakes but when they pile up, it’s not the same.” Spanish media report that Asencio expects to be cleared in the video sharing case if the two young women who were filmed, aged 16 and 18, formally forgive him. Three former Real Madrid reserve players are also on trial for allegedly recording and distributing the video. The trial is scheduled for September 3, 4 and 7. Asencio suffered a hamstring injury in July and has yet to be picked for a matchday squad by his new coach. But he played regularly for Real in the previous two seasons. The post Real Madrid open disciplinary proceedings against Asencio appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Should We Be Afraid of Our Food?
items.description: T he cyclosporiasis outbreak that has garnered so much attention in recent months is unquestionably bad news. People have been sickened in at least 48 states, and the number of lab-confirmed cases—about 17,000—represents only a fraction of the number of people who have been infected by the parasite. But as foodborne illnesses go, a cyclospora infection—most likely caused in this instance by the consumption of iceberg lettuce contaminated with human feces—is relatively mild: unpleasant but rarely life-threatening. The two people who have died during the current outbreak had serious underlying conditions. Other foodborne pathogens are far more dangerous. More than 1 million Americans are sickened by Salmonella every year; invasive, potentially life- threatening infections occur in about 8 percent of lab-confirmed cases, and cause meningitis, sepsis, and other serious complications. A botulism infection can cause paralysis, seizures, nerve damage, lung damage, and brain damage, as well as death. A few years ago, I reported here on an outbreak of Cronobacter infections linked to powdered infant formula and the subsequent recall by Abbott Nutrition. Two recent botulism outbreaks linked to powdered infant formula made by two other companies have thus far received little attention. During an outbreak that peaked in November 2025, at least 48 infants across 17 states were stricken with botulism traced to powdered formula from the company ByHeart. The infants were hospitalized with severe complications; one of them suffered multiple strokes. Then, earlier this year, at least four infants in three states were stricken with botulism from powdered formula made by the company Nara Organics. All four infants were hospitalized. [ Read: The worst part of the cyclosporiasis response ] A key ingredient in the tainted formula sold by both companies was milk powder from a common supplier —the likely carrier of the botulism spores. Today’s powdered formula is highly industrialized, with dozens of ingredients from multiple sources. The contents of a single can of formula may contain milk from thousands of different cows. Nobody has ever fed babies this kind of stuff before. From December 2025 through February 2026, more than 100 infants in at least 10 countries were sickened in all likelihood by powdered formula tainted with spores from the bacterium Bacillus cereus . The formula, manufactured by several different companies, including Nestlé and Danone , had been contaminated by a fatty-acid additive supplied by a biotech firm in Wuhan, China. A generation ago, an outbreak of food poisoning generally remained small-scale. The source was likely to be tainted ground beef from a local butcher shop or an egg salad gone bad at a church picnic. As the scale of industrial food production has grown, so has the scale of foodborne outbreaks. When I wrote my book Fast Food Nation , published in 2001, high levels of fecal contamination of ground beef were already a nationwide problem, not just a local one, because huge ground-beef-processing plants with poor safety procedures were supplying the fast-food industry. The dairy industry now presents similar problems of scale. The supply chain for the botulism-tainted infant formula went like this: 55 dairies in California sold raw milk to a company called Organic West; that raw milk was then shipped from California to an enormous plant operated by Dairy Farmers of America in Fallon, Nevada, and processed into milk powder. For ByHeart, the powder was shipped to a plant in Iowa, turned into formula, shipped to Oregon for additional processing, packaged there, and sold throughout the United States. For Nara Organics, the milk powder was shipped from Nevada to Germany, manufactured into formula, shipped to Denmark, packaged, and shipped back to the U.S. Government never adapts quickly, and because policies are adopted piecemeal over decades, many federal food-safety rules make little sense . For instance, frozen cheese pizzas are regulated by the FDA—but if a frozen pizza has a lot of pepperoni or other meats, it’s regulated by the Department of Agriculture. The U.S. is the only developed country that divides responsibility for food safety among separate government agencies. So it is hardly surprising that monitoring and enforcement have not kept up with changes in food production. The larger problem is that the food-safety system we have—underfunded for decades—is being methodically dismantled by the Trump administration. The FDA is responsible for the safety of about 80 percent of the food consumed in the United States. Last year, James Jones, the highly respected head of the FDA’s human-foods division, resigned from his post , citing the “indiscriminate” firing of 89 staff members. The loss of such expertise threatens to cripple the agency’s food-safety efforts. Kyle Diamantas—who replaced Jones and now serves as the acting head of the FDA—has no scientific, medical, or public-health training. He is an attorney (and Donald Trump Jr.’s hunting companion). While employed at the law firm Jones Day, Diamantas defended Abbott Laboratories in a lawsuit alleging that the company had knowingly sold infant formula that could cause severe bowel problems. Abbott lost the suit and in August agreed to pay a $670 million settlement to resolve that case and other claims. In a statement to investors , Abbott said that the settlement is “not in any way an admission of liability” and that the company “remains confident in the safety of these products.” The USDA, which has food-safety oversight of meat, eggs, and poultry, has also suffered significant cutbacks under Donald Trump, losing about one-fifth of its workforce in 2025. At the CDC, the chief food-safety expert, Daniel Jernigan, resigned in August 2025 , angered by budget cuts and political interference. The number of pathogens tracked by FoodNet, a crucial CDC surveillance program, has been cut by 75 percent. The amount of money spent on FoodNet annually is a fraction of what has already been spent to renovate the Reflecting Pool in front of the Lincoln Memorial. D uring the late 1890s, tainted and adulterated food was commonplace in the United States. Upton Sinclair’s muckraking 1906 novel, The Jungle , exposed a variety of noxious practices—such as making sausage from rats—and prompted President Theodore Roosevelt to support food-safety legislation. The food industry vehemently opposed Roosevelt: “We are paying all we care to pay,” one executive told Congress. The industry lost that battle—federal agencies gained regulatory power—but continues to fight back. It spends more on lobbying and political donations than the oil or defense industries do. The tragedy is that public-health experts agree on many of the straightforward steps that should be taken to ensure food safety. And they can point to a record of success. In 2002, a year after the publication of Fast Food Nation , I met a woman named Barbara Kowalcyk, whose 2-year-old son, Kevin, had recently died after being infected with E. coli O157:H7 from a tainted hamburger. It was an all-too-frequent occurrence back then—nationwide outbreaks of E. coli O157:H7 were routinely caused by ground beef. Kowalcyk was determined that other parents should never have to endure her experience. Trained as a biostatistician, she returned to school and earned a doctorate in environmental science and food safety. She is now a professor at George Washington University’s school of public health. A decade after we met, Kowalcyk played a leading role in campaigning for “test and hold,” a food-safety rule to prevent meat companies from shipping ground beef until it had tested negative for dangerous forms of E. coli . In 2013, the rule was finally adopted by the USDA. Few large E. coli outbreaks are today caused by ground beef. [ Eric Schlosser: Do we really want a food cartel? ] Similar test-and-hold rules could help eliminate Salmonella from poultry. A 2022 study by Consumer Reports found that almost one-third of the ground chicken sold at American supermarkets contained Salmonella —an extraordinarily high level. Strict food-safety regulation of the poultry industry in Denmark has reduced the level of Salmonella contamination in broiler chickens there from 14 to 0.3 percent—and, as a result, the number of people sickened by Salmonella has declined by 99.6 percent. But the Trump administration recently blocked the adoption of a new rule, about to go in effect after years of deliberation at the USDA, that would have prohibited the sale of poultry products highly contaminated with Salmonella , claiming the rule would have imposed “significant financial and operational burdens on American businesses and consumers.” The Meat Institute and the National Chicken Council backed the move. When it comes to food manufactured for infants, the federal government has enormous leverage that is going unused. The infant-formula industry is highly concentrated. Two companies, Abbott and Mead Johnson, control more than 80 percent of the market. Through the USDA’s Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children, or WIC, the federal government buys more than half of the infant formula consumed in the United States—meaning that it could swiftly mandate changes on behalf of infant health. But it hasn’t. The Republican-controlled Congress has refused to hold hearings on the botulism outbreaks or on legislation introduced in March that would expand pathogen testing of infant formula and strengthen congressional oversight . The idea of putting all federal food-safety efforts under one roof is a nonstarter. “We are paying all we care to pay”—that was the industry response in 1906, and that is the response today. It’s the rest of us who bear the cost.

items.title: Creating the Perfect Female Monster
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts The breakout crime drama Furious opens with a scene that’s hard to watch: Catherine, a serial killer played by Lola Petticrew, is keeping a man prisoner in a row house and taunting him as he dies: “I don’t like the sounds you’re making.” The show’s creator, Liz Meriwether, is announcing right away that you will be spending time with a monster, and the discomfort amps up from there. As the show progresses, we learn that Catherine has been trafficked, and the men she is killing were involved in her abuse. In an era when “Epstein Island” exists, Catherine represents a specific kind of psychopathic serial killer. She is, as the title suggests, one of the Furies exacting revenge in a world that hasn’t managed to execute justice for her the legal way. Meriwether says she did not set out to make a statement on the state of female rage or American justice, or even a commentary on Epstein, yet the show may have hit a nerve because those issues are so alive right now. Nine years ago, women’s anger fueled the MeToo movement, and it seemed as if the way society confronts sexual harassment and abuse was on the brink of transformation. “Misogyny is more overt on the internet than it’s ever been,” the Atlantic staff writer Sophie Gilbert says. “And you think about what happened to that anger and what happened to that rage, and I know from my own perspective, you can’t live with that kind of anger for a decade. You just can’t. It has to burn out. It has to go somewhere, or you just get numb.” In this episode, Meriwether talks about the complications of humanizing a serial killer and how the project of creating complicated women characters has evolved in her decade of writing for television. And Gilbert talks about what it means that more women creators are owning the stories told about women. The following is a transcript of the episode: Hanna Rosin: A female monster is a rare but recurring creature. She often emerges at moments in history when women in society are collectively angry at the powers that be but unable to express it. Maybe they’re too defeated or maybe numb, so the monster gets revenge for them. I’m Hanna Rosin. This is Radio Atlantic . Right now, there is a particularly interesting monster out there taking revenge on a fictional Jeffrey Epstein. It’s playing out on the Hulu show Furious —the season finale aired this week. Sophie Gilbert: Well, it was one of those shows that became a slow burn, I think. [ Theme song from Furious] Rosin: This is staff writer Sophie Gilbert. Gilbert: When it first debuted, there wasn’t that much chatter about it. But then you started to see people watch, and it became this word-of-mouth hit. Rosin: Furious is a dark and sometimes disturbing TV show about a female serial killer, played by Lola Petticrew, who is pursued by a female FBI agent, played by Emmy Rossum. Gilbert: So there’s a lot about it that is quite kind of tropey, old-school procedural. It’s a crime show. The cop and the killer being pursued, they have that kind of, Oh, we’re not so different, you and I , kind of thing going on. But at the same time, it was also like no other procedural I’ve ever seen, in the sense that in so many crime shows, you see women’s bodies used like window dressing almost. And this is a show that really seems to be made about women, not for women necessarily, but it’s interested in women. It’s interested in what happens to women when they go through traumatic experiences, what happens to women when they become angry. There’s so much that is kind of really deep and tied to these mythological elements of transformation and violence. And it just works well on so many levels. Rosin: The show’s mythological elements are in the name. It’s called Furious after the Furies, the Greek goddesses of vengeance. In the show, the Furies are implied to be serial killer Catherine, FBI agent Alice, and Alice’s mentor, Nora—three women who, in different ways, have all failed to find the justice they need. Gilbert: So Nora Washington is the head of the FBI’s sex-crimes unit in the show. She’s played by Quincy Tyler Bernstine in this extraordinary performance. She’s so good. And she has a few speeches where she’s talking to Alice Black, sort of the main character in the show, who’s played by Emmy Rossum, who is trying to become an FBI agent under her wing. And she’s explaining to her the toll that this job takes, of looking into these horrendous sex crimes, these crimes often against underage girls, against children. You take on this responsibility when you do this job of doing this thing that no one else will do, to try and achieve a measure of justice, or certainly a measure of justice that is often impossible, and it changes you. Quincy Tyler Bernstine (as Nora Washington in Furious): Everyone likes it when there’s a sweet little woman lying on the floor, naked and cut up in pieces. I get so fucking angry. Gilbert: Because you have to become, in some ways, a monster to do this day after day. Bernstine: It doesn’t matter, anything you do. The ones who are really to blame don’t get caught. Never. Never. Gilbert: So there are all these sort of elemental themes of Greek tragedy and Greek drama that seem to come through. Bernstine: You think you’re ever gonna catch anyone who matters? Gilbert: So this show starts with a scene of a woman whose name we later find out is Catherine—she’s played by Lola Petticrew—who is keeping a man prisoner in a Brooklyn row house on Halloween. [ Sounds from Furious] Gilbert: And Catherine is wearing a mask, and she is eating candy corn, and she is clearly torturing this man. And then eventually, we see her murder him. Lola Petticrew (as Catherine Grace in Furious): I don’t really like listening to you. I don’t like the sounds you’re making. Gilbert: And the show begins in this really stark way of saying, This is who this character is . Like, Be horrified by this; be appalled by her actions . It’s sort of really uncomfortable to watch in lots of ways, really visceral. And then as the show goes on, you understand more about who she is. You understand her history. You understand why she’s doing what she’s doing, her flawed but in some ways very sympathetic logic. And you see her full humanity. And she becomes, yes, a serial killer, but one who does seem to be doing it for reasons that are, if not fully justifiable, you start to sort of empathize with them a little bit more. Rosin: Yeah. And here’s the difficult thing: The parallels to the current world are apparent. This is essentially a Jeffrey Epstein setup. It’s a setup about people who are portrayed as rich. There’s a man at the center of it. There’s a sort of a twisted luring in of teenagers and young women. It really has obvious parallels to the world we are currently living in. And here’s a woman exacting justice because the justice system wouldn’t. Gilbert: Yes. Rosin: So as I describe it, it is sympathetic. You are, in some ways, supposed to root for this person who at the very first scene is gruesome. Gilbert: I don’t know if you’re supposed to root for her, but it becomes impossible not to, in some ways. Rosin: Yeah, yeah. Gilbert: And I think that’s part of the trick. The show is not black and white morally. It reveals things, and it explains them, and it offers context for them. And we, as human beings, watch it, and we have our own context, and we have our own life experiences, and we add. And we’re supposed to make our own judgments, but I don’t think the show is telling us what to sort of presume one way or another. And that, to me, is what makes it so interesting as an experience. But yes, this character Jay Easton is, obviously—he’s certainly in the Jeffrey Epstein mold. He’s a billionaire. He’s revealed to have preyed on hundreds, maybe thousands of young, underage women. And yet, what again is striking about the show is that he’s not really interesting. He’s not a character who the show is sort of interested in delving into, really. The show is much more curious about the impact he’s had on the lives of women and girls, and that, I think, is often what goes underplayed or what is missing in our Epstein discourse as well. So it’s shining a light on a different facet of this very topical issue. [ Music ] Rosin: As I watched episode after episode, I had a very uncomfortable reaction that I’m guessing other people had, that the creator of the show, Liz Meriwether—who we’ll talk to later—says she intended: I was not, not rooting for the serial killer, this deeply unlikeable, twisted, dark, criminal young woman who was effectively hunting down the men who had abused her when she was a teenager. Gilbert: Without being, like, morally endorsing murder, it can be cathartic to see where they go with it and to imagine what happens when there’s no justice possible. What do you do with all that rage? Rosin: Sophie wrote about the show recently for The Atlantic , about how the grief, anger, and rage in Furious reminded her of a different time, nearly a decade ago, when similar feelings of anger generated headlines, spawned think pieces and hashtags, and started the MeToo movement that ultimately fizzled out. Rosin: Yeah. So what does that reflect in the culture then? A sense of frustration, helplessness? What does that mean? Gilbert: For me, the show really resonated when I was thinking about—first of all, it’s been almost a decade since the MeToo moment, which is just wild to think about anyway, all this time. But when you think about what happened at the end of 2017, the revelations about Harvey Weinstein, the revelations about all these men— Reporter (from ABC News): New Yorker magazine reporting new claims of sexual harassment, assault, and rape. One of his accusers going to police, secretly recording her confrontation with Weinstein, but no charges were ever filed. Gilbert: —there was so much in the sense that we were in this moment of societal transformation and women’s anger. There were so many books written about women’s anger. There were TV shows written about women’s anger. It seemed like rage and fury, and righteous fury, was this great theme in our culture that might have a kind of revolutionary force, that it might help upend systems and overturn injustice. Reporter (from CBS Miami): Instead of naming one person, Time magazine named its 2017 Person of the Year the “silence breakers,” the name given to the women who came forward to report sexual harassment and assault, sparking the MeToo moveme nt. Gilbert: And then you look nine years later and you think, Wow, actually, none of that has happened. We’ve, if anything, lost rights . Misogyny is more overt on the internet than it’s ever been. More and more injustices and horrific crimes against women and girls are revealed. I mean, really, it feels almost daily. We have an overtly misogynist president, I would say. And you think about what happened to that anger and what happened to that rage, and I know from my own perspective, you can’t live with that kind of anger for a decade. You just can’t. It has to burn out. It has to go somewhere, or you just get numb, I think. And so what this show is doing, which really connected with my own sense of just being unable to feel that rage day after day after day, is wondering what happens when it becomes something else, when it takes a different direction, when it realizes that justice is impossible, and so vengeance is the next best thing. Rosin: Hmm. I wanna ask about the broad sweep of things. In your book, Girl on Girl , the thesis is that pop culture taught Millennial women to hate themselves, or maybe just that pop culture of the ’90s and aughts hated women in a certain way. This is a show conceived of by women, written by women, in which a woman and the Furies do get revenge. Does that at least agency, even if it’s a perverse agency, does that represent something different, like controlling the narrative? Gilbert: Yes, the stories that we get now about women, about the complexities of their lives, the conditions that they’re living under, like the truth of their experience, are made by women about women. There’s so much that is so much better than it was even 10 years ago. And I was reading an interview with Liz Meriwether, the creator of Furious , where she said—because she’s the creator of a much-beloved sitcom, one of my favorites, called New Girl —and she was mentioning the notes that she got from Fox in terms of sort of making the character more likable and making it broadly more appealing to men, and how now, making this show, Furious , there was none of that. There’s much more appetite I think, or at least more understanding on the part of people commissioning work like this, that you can be interested in women as a subject and that will make great art that will connect with viewers and be enough of a justification. We don’t need to always be kind of shushing women in a way. Rosin: Yeah. And it’s not just, you can be interested in women. You can be interested—I mean, the task she’s setting out for a viewer here is: You can be interested in a woman who’s, like you said, a monster. From the very first scene, she’s the exact opposite of a beautiful dead victim. She couldn’t be less likable, at least in the very beginning. Gilbert: Yes. And the show really trusts us as audiences to see that and to keep watching, which I think is fascinating all on its own. Like, there’s this idea that we don’t need to be coddled into finding this woman cute and sexy. ( Laughs .) Rosin: Yeah. Gilbert: We can see what she is and we can be hooked anyway, because we’re sophisticated enough consumers of media to understand that the payoff might be worth it. [ Music ] Rosin: After the break, we talk to the Furious showrunner, Liz Meriwether, about why she created a monster you don’t necessarily hate. [ Break ] [ Music ] Rosin: Liz Merriweather started as a comedy writer. As Sophie mentioned, her breakout hit was New Girl . Then she wrote The Dropout , a show about Theranos founder and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes—also not a classic lovable type. And then Dying for Sex , about a woman who has a terminal-cancer diagnosis—so potentially a perfect victim—but instead, she decides to spend her final months having a lot of sex. We’ve talked a lot on this episode about post-MeToo progress being stalled. But this—this creation, by female writers, of female characters who test the bounds of likeability—is also a kind of progress. I talk to Merriweather—who is in the writers’ room working on Season 2 of Furious —about how her ability to write female characters exactly how she wants them has evolved. [ Music ] So the terrible word that’s imposed on female characters forever, which is likable — female politicians, everybody, likability —from the very first scene, you make the decision to make Catherine not likable. Did you get any pushback on that? Like, Put some woman in there who is more pure, or a sort of more recognizable person you can attach yourself to ? Meriwether: As somebody who’s been doing this for about 15 years now, and when I first started doing it, got that note all the time, I was surprised that I didn’t get that note. Rosin: Can you actually talk about that? ’Cause you were mostly known as a comedy writer. New Girl was the breakout hit, and when you were writing that, what were the conversations like about how weird or unconventional a main character who’s a woman could be? Meriwether: Yeah. The notes I got were, like—the first pilot I wrote was called Sluts . It was kind of Girls before Girls , in a way. It was three girls in New York who just, like, had a lot of sex and just were deciding to get their lives together and sort of stop having so much sex. And this was for Fox. It was never gonna get on the air. But that was the first pilot that I wrote, and I had conversations with executives that were like, She either is smart, or she likes sex , and that was a binary thing that I had to genuinely have a conversation with somebody about. Where I was like, No, you can be smart and also have had a lot of sex . Rosin: So you were in your 20s when you wrote that pilot, when you wrote Sluts . Meriwether: Yeah, I was, like, 25 or something. Yeah. Rosin: And did you already know, I’m trying to push against some kind of tropes or ideas of how female characters should be ? Meriwether: Yeah. I mean, I think I’ve always come from a place of, like, I’m gonna make jokes about it or try to come at it from a little bit of a sneakier place. I’ve never been a writer that’s been very I have a big statement I wanna make . Which is, honestly, why this show kinda scared me a little bit, because I was like, I don’t get to hide as much . I don’t get to kind of, like, you know, tap-dance and make jokes and say, like, No, look over here. Look over here. Look over here. But yes, I’ve always been interested in trying to put women on screen that are not what you have seen before. That’s been something that I’ve been interested in for a long time. I just feel like we’ve taken steps forward and steps back over the past 15 years, but there’s definitely more complicated female characters on television now than there was back then. When New Girl first aired, I did a lot of press. It was, like, me and Whitney Cummings had comedies coming out, and [people] were like, We can’t believe there are, like, comedies written by women—more than one comedy written by women . That was like the main thrust of the press. And that would never be a story nowadays. So yes, there, I mean, there is growth. I think that there’s also a lot of moving forward then moving backwards. Rosin: Yeah. For this episode, we also interviewed my Atlantic colleague Sophie Gilbert, who wrote this book Girl on Girl , which is about how pop culture of the late ’90s and aughts hated women or taught Millennial women to hate themselves. And I was thinking about you because you, that’s your era of pop culture. I also saw that you signed on to write the biopic of Britney Spears, who is the ultimate example of how the late ’90s and early aughts chewed some women up. And so I wondered if that was part of what motivates you or what excites you about these kinds of projects. Meriwether: I think so. Yeah. I mean, I do kinda just keep my head down and keep moving forward. Like, I don’t go from a place of like I have an agenda . But yes, those are the characters that really excite me—the women where it’s, like, very hard to put into words how you feel about them. You don’t know if you’re rooting for them or not. I do think it’s a very interesting, fun place to be as a writer, maybe because of all of the notes I got about likability and the desire to sort of get away from that. But I also think it’s not interesting to make somebody completely evil. I think that middle space is really interesting. Rosin: And maybe it just feels more true. Meriwether: Yeah. There’s also a tendency to, say, victimize women in a different way, where it’s like they had no agency in what happened to them or, you know, they are completely products of a broken system, which I feel like is not fair either and a little bit patronizing and boring, honestly. So I think I’m interested in, like, all the nuances of why people do the things they do. [ Music ] Rosin: Sophie, you know what I was thinking about? The Olivia Rodrigo reprisal of Lilith Fair. Olivia Rodrigo : 45,000 people at this festival tonight. Can you believe it? Rosin: I don’t know if you saw the documentary about Lilith Fair. Gilbert: I did, yeah. Rosin: So I watched that documentary, and I think I might have cried, honestly, because I thought, Oh, well, that era is dead . Like, We will never, ever have that back again. [ Sounds from the Lilith Fair: Building a Mystery trailer ] Rosin: A sort of collection of women getting together, talking about their music, entirely made for and run by women, and yet here it is reprised this summer. And I thought, Oh, maybe the sense of agency that’s emerging, it does feel different than what you wrote about [in your book] . It does feel different than the Britney Spears era, the era in which women died by those cultural stories. Now it feels like they’re writing the stories, and so even though they might be grim or they might be inspirational, they are controlling the narrative. Gilbert: That Lilith documentary was so good and I think so sad, for exactly the reasons that you said, which was: It seemed the last moment when this idea of a women-centric society, or at least an alternative society, seemed possible. ( Laughs .) And then everything that happened afterwards in the 2000s, and just this real decade of victimizing women for living their lives in public. But yes, again, we have this moment of a mainstream pop star holding a massive music festival for abortion-rights charities and reproductive rights, which you can’t imagine someone like Taylor Swift doing that. Rodrigo: Today I’m so aware of all the women who came before me, who fought for me to enjoy the rights that I enjoy today. Gilbert: All right, it’s not as subversive and as edgy as what riot-grrrl musicians were doing in the ’90s, but it’s political. It’s active. It’s angry about the way that things are, and it’s willing to take a stand to change them. And then it also—I think the thing that I found so fascinating about this festival, Daisy Chain, was that it just demonstrates the power that women have in the music industry. Of all the different cultural industries, music really seems to be one where women are dominant right now—where they sell the most records, where they’re making the most interesting music, where they’re the ones that we are drawn to. They have these huge tours, and they have this huge fandom, and they are front and center in music and powerful in a way that men are not. And that, I think, is interesting right now, in this moment. And the question of why, I don’t know. But if we’re looking for things to be hopeful about, that’s definitely one. Rosin: Right, ’cause in thinking about women’s anger, I got stuck in a kind of limited narrative, which is, Oh, in 2017, women were able to channel the anger in a productive direction . People told their stories. Sort of a dam burst open. There were truths out there, and that was cathartic. And in 2026, we get a serial killer. So then I was trying to think, Well, maybe that’s not that simple . There are places that anger finds an out that are more joyful or productive, and so this is one that I look to. Gilbert: Yeah. Olivia Rodrigo just released a song called “Serena Joy,” which is named, obviously, after the character in The Handmaid’s Tale who has helped subjugate other women. One of the lyrics in it is, “If you can’t throw a punch, you can learn how to spit.” [“Serena Joy,” by Olivia Rodrigo] Gilbert: Just, it’s this idea that numbness is not inevitable. We don’t have to just be complacent forever and ever and ever while our rights are eroded and things are taken away—that in some ways, cultural power is still there, and that there are still women sort of taking a stand for things, and in some ways, storytelling is able to do such interesting work now because we are in a different place than we were in 2017, and we’re much more open to ideas about what’s possible, even if it doesn’t seem like it’s easily achievable. Rosin: Yeah. Well, Sophie, thank you so much for talking this through with me today. Gilbert: Oh, it’s a pleasure. Thank you for having me. [ Music ] Rosin: This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Rosie Hughes and Jinae West with help from Jacob Smollen. It was edited by Claudine Ebeid. Rob Smierciak engineered and provided original music. We also had music from Breakmaster Cylinder. Fact-checking by Sam Fentress. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. Listeners, if you enjoy the show, you can support our work and the work of all Atlantic journalists when you subscribe to The Atlantic at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. I’m Hanna Rosin. Thank you for listening.

items.title: How ‘Somatics’ Became the Solution to Modern Life
items.description: When clients go to Sybil Ottenstein for therapy, they tend to arrive with answers. Many of them have seen shrinks before. They can tell her which events from their past were formative, and point to the ripple effects in their current life. They’re like detectives, she told me, with all the dots connected on their corkboard of evidence. Intellectually, they’ve cracked the case. The problem is that they don’t feel any better. That’s why they’re seeking something different from Ottenstein: somatic psychotherapy. Traditional talk therapy could be seen as a top-down approach. You identify problems in your thinking, your habits, or your life, and hope that by working through them, you can resolve physical manifestations of emotional issues—the chest palpitations of anxiety, the stomachache of stress. Somatic therapy, by contrast, works from the bottom up. Ottenstein typically starts her sessions by asking clients to slow down and pay attention to corporeal sensations: “What does it feel like in your chest? In your throat?” As they talk, she encourages them to stay in their body, to let themselves feel whatever is coming up. People cry. They yawn. They scream. They stretch. They dance. The word somatic , according to Merriam-Webster , merely means “of, relating to, or affecting the body.” But recently, it’s been popping up everywhere, appended to a variety of practices that involve tuning in to physical symptoms in order to ameliorate psychological ones. Somatic therapists like Ottenstein have noticed a significant bump in interest; one of the major somatic-therapy training programs reported that its applicants more than doubled from 2020 to 2023. Other practitioners offer somatic dance, somatic yoga, somatic workouts. (The terms seem a touch redundant.) [ Read: How did healing ourselves get so exhausting? ] On Instagram, hundreds of thousands of posts appear with the hashtag #somatic. A “somatic exercise” trainer who goes by the “Workout Witch” (nearly 2 million followers) teaches small, repetitive movements meant to discharge negative feelings—curl your head down for “sorrow/despair,” pull your right ear for “overwhelm”—and promises that “trauma can be released from your hips.” All over my feed, fit young women are humming , hitting their sternum, pinching their nose bridge, and bouncing their knees all the way to inner peace. [ Read: These Millennials can’t get out of their head ] Much of the time, as with many other wellness ventures, someone stands to make money. At one somatic-workout class I attended, where a staffer told me that the goal was to “move stagnant energy out,” the lobby featured a gift-shop corner with jewelry, T-shirts, and $65 “body gloss” from a brand called Oui the People. But clearly, plenty of Americans are willing to pay for the promise of a psychic cleanse. Practitioners refer to “stuck energy,” to “ trapped emotions ,” to “resetting” a nervous system caught in fight-or-flight mode. “We have all these ways of just storing that gunk inside,” Ottenstein told me. I pictured, uncomfortably, a thick, black goo running through my veins. Somatics—the whole roomy umbrella of practices—might seem like an odd fit for the information age, when people are more accustomed to finding answers on the internet than within themselves. But that could be precisely the draw for thinkers and analyzers who are tired of ruminating in anxious circles, who spend their days in front of a laptop and nights scrolling an iPhone. For millennia, people have yearned to break out of the confines of their bodies; they’ve searched—through religion, spirituality, drugs—for transcendence. Now, for some, the existential quest is inverted: Instead of seeking to escape their prison of flesh and bones, they want to reinhabit it. The origin of somatics is difficult to pinpoint, though it’s certainly not recent. Some credit Wilhelm Reich, a student of Freud’s, who theorized in the early 1900s that patients held tension in their bodies—“muscular armor”—as a subconscious defense against trauma, leading to aches, pains, and inflammation. But it wasn’t until the 1970s that the field began to formalize, developed in part by the American philosophy professor Thomas Hanna, who defined somatics as the study of “the body as perceived from within.” That same decade, a UC Berkeley biophysics doctoral student, Peter Levine, developed “somatic experiencing”: a therapeutic method based on the idea that people, like other animals, react to trauma with a flight, fight, or freeze response, powered by a burst of adrenaline. After the source of danger is gone, Levine argued, they have pent-up “survival energy” to unleash: They need to physically shake it off. He pointed to videos of impalas, quaking and buckling after surviving a cheetah attack. When humans go through something upsetting, Ottenstein told me, “we go to work the next day.” This idea—that trauma is held in the body, and thus must be physically remedied—was once fairly niche. In recent years, though, it has been jolted into prominence. The psychiatrist Bessel van der Kolk’s book The Body Keeps the Score , which argues for somatic treatments of PTSD, was first released in 2014 and was not an immediate hit. In 2021, it reached the No. 1 spot on the New York Times best-seller list for paperback nonfiction. And although it has been accused of resting on shaky science, it has continued to dominate the charts for years. Van der Kolk wrote about violent assaults, wartime atrocities, severe childhood abuse—circumstances that many readers hadn’t directly experienced. Yet The Body Keeps the Score seemed to resonate anyway. When it gained momentum, lots of Americans had spent the previous year safe in their homes, baking bread and taking Zoom calls. (“When people say the pandemic has been a collective trauma,” van der Kolk told The Atlantic that year, “I say, absolutely not.”) Most had also, however, been detached from the rich sensory experience of interacting with the external world. Now here was a book about people who’d felt estranged from their own body—and then, through simple movement, play, and touch, found their way back to their surroundings, and to themselves. [ Read: The self-help that no one needs right now ] In the years since, most people have emerged from pandemic isolation. Yet the share of Americans who say they frequently experience stress, which has been rising for decades, has continued its upward trend. Talk therapy remains popular, but it’s not always affordable or accessible—and much of the time, it doesn’t take physical symptoms into account. Meanwhile, many medical doctors don’t consider psychological causes of physical ailments. Stress in particular is “like this mythical creature,” Aditi Nerurkar, a physician at Harvard Medical School, told me. “And we don’t have a lot of time. We have to focus on your hemoglobin. Did you get a mammogram? Did you get a pap smear? What is your cholesterol? ” No wonder, then, that somatics is a flourishing industry. Many Americans already distrust medical institutions; maybe they want to bypass the dismissive doctor, or the therapist who wants to rehash every daddy issue but can’t seem to fix anything. So they turn to this strange constellation of New Age–y courses, TikTok sages, and licensed counselors. Some offerings target people with capital- T Trauma; others claim to be for just about anyone. Many present themselves as alternatives to more traditional paths to mental well-being. The question is whether they can really help the frazzled masses. Somatics does get a lot of things right. Plenty of bodily sensations are, at root, psychological. Some communication does need to happen between the brain and the rest of the body. That’s how you know to respond to danger: The amygdala triggers the nervous system to increase your heart rate, deliver more blood to muscles, and release a flood of adrenaline. When I spoke with Nerurkar, she rattled off an incomplete list of physical symptoms that might result from stress: headaches, dizziness, nausea, vision changes. When she was in residency training, she said, she experienced what felt like a “stampede of wild horses” across her chest and was convinced that she had a heart problem—until her doctors, having conducted a battery of tests, recommended that she seriously consider chilling out. And many components of somatic practice have evidence to back them up. Interoception , or awareness of one’s own physical signals, really can be important for well-being—perhaps because it increases people’s sense of attunement with their body, connection with the present moment, or agency over otherwise vague and inscrutable sensations. Mindfulness meditation, which involves interoception, has been shown to decrease stress and anxiety and even reduce physical pain. Yoga and breathing exercises can decrease amygdala activation and lead to better concentration, memory, and executive function. But the somatics packaging of these techniques is alluring partly because of the emotional liberation it promises. Somaticists tend to describe a clear path: identify a physical signal, connect it to its psychic cause, then let it go . If the nervous system overactivates, surely you can just reset it. If the body holds trauma, surely the body can relinquish it. These were always just metaphors, though, and imperfect ones. The amygdala doesn’t have a reboot button. There is no viscous gunk of emotional pain to flush out. The Body Keeps the Score has been somewhat debunked; critics have argued that van der Kolk incorrectly described certain studies, and that he seems to have made up others entirely. (Responding to the writer Emi Nietfeld’s critique in Mother Jones , van der Kolk said that at times he drew on unpublished data.) Trauma experts have pushed back on his wholesale condemnation of talk therapy, which can be, according to a mountain of evidence, very helpful for treating PTSD. There’s also something ironic in how certain somaticists—ostensibly advocates for the mind-body connection—talk as if the two are separated by a nearly unbridgeable gap: the physical burden of trauma unreachable through thinking or conversation, and perhaps not even accessible to conscious awareness. [ Read: Why we’re still talking about the ‘trauma plot’ ] So somatics isn’t a miracle cure. And it’s probably right to be skeptical of influencers who seek to collect on people’s need to feel at home in their body. But that doesn’t mean somatics can’t be helpful. Much of it, after all, turns out to be pretty straightforward. Movement is good, generally. Breathing is good. Stepping away from your screen—stretching your limbs, remembering you are real and tangible and mortal—is good. When I signed up for that somatic-exercise class, I expected that I might leave rolling my eyes , but I secretly hoped I’d walk out lighter, more alive and connected to myself and the world. What I found was something in between. The actual workout couldn’t have been more basic: It consisted largely of squats, jumping jacks, crunches, some yoga—downward dog, child’s pose. Occasionally the instructor would remind us to check in with our bodies: “What are you being invited into? And I don’t mean the burpee.” Or: “Let the chin enter the conversation.” Otherwise it hardly seemed uniquely somatic , or uniquely anything. Then again, I had the post-workout endorphin glow. I’d left my apartment and shut my phone in a locker. An hour later, I exited the studio somewhat baffled. But walking out onto a busy Manhattan street, I felt a little more conscious of the sun on my cheek, the solidness of the ground pushing against my feet. This was silly , I thought. And also: Maybe I’ll come back . ​​When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic

items.title: Only 35% of 2026 BECE candidates scored aggregates 6–24 – CSSPS
items.description: Only about 35 per cent of candidates who sat the 2026 Basic Education Certificate Examination (BECE) obtained aggregates ranging from six to 24, according to the Computerised School Selection and Placement System (CSSPS). The Coordinator of the CSSPS, Sherif Sulemana, on JoyFM’s Super Morning Show on Thursday, September 3, said approximately 252,000 candidates fell within the aggregate-six-to-24 category. “You only had about 252,000 or so, or about 35 per cent of the candidates, getting from aggregate six to 24,” he said. He further disclosed that only 17 per cent of the candidates, representing approximately 107,000 students, obtained aggregates between six and 18. “If you look at the data on the performance of the candidates, we only had about 17 per cent of the candidates getting from aggregate six to 18. In absolute figures, you are talking about about 107,000,” he stated. Mr Sulemana said an estimated 620,000 candidates sat the examination, of whom about 565,000 qualified to participate in the placement exercise. This means approximately 55,000 candidates are expected to be excluded from placement into second-cycle institutions. According to him, candidates who failed either English Language or Mathematics do not qualify for placement. “You are disqualified from placement if you have failed either English or Mathematics,” he explained. Mr Sulemana also clarified that Grade 9 does not automatically indicate failure under the standardised grading system. He said candidates’ raw examination scores are taken into account when determining whether they have met the qualification requirements. Ahead of the placement exercise, the CSSPS has activated call centres to assist candidates and parents with placement-related concerns. Mr Sulemana said people who live far from the regional resolution centres could contact the call centres to report their challenges and receive assistance. “If you are in a district far from the regional centre, all you have to do is call the call centre, let them understand your issue, and that will be resolved for you,” he said.

items.title: Only 17% of 2026 BECE candidates score aggregates 6–18 – CSSPS
items.description: Only 17 per cent of candidates who sat the 2026 Basic Education Certificate Examination (BECE) obtained aggregates ranging from six to 18, according to the Computerised School Selection and Placement System (CSSPS). The Coordinator of the CSSPS, Sherif Sulemana, said the figure translates into approximately 107,000 candidates out of the estimated 620,000 who sat the examination. “If you look at the data on the performance of the candidates, we only had about 17 per cent of the candidates getting an aggregate of six to 18. In absolute figures, you are talking about 107,000,” he disclosed on JoyFM’s SMS on Thursday, September 3. Mr Sulemana also disclosed that approximately 252,000 candidates obtained aggregates ranging from six to 24. His comments highlight the performance spread among candidates ahead of the placement exercise into second-cycle institutions. According to him, about 565,000 candidates have qualified for placement this year, while approximately 55,000 will not be placed. “Based on our analysis, we have about 565,000 qualified for placement this year,” he stated. Mr Sulemana explained that candidates who failed either English Language or Mathematics were not eligible for placement. “You are disqualified from placement if you have failed either English or Mathematics,” he said. He clarified that obtaining Grade 9 under the standardised grading system did not, by itself, mean a candidate had failed. The candidate’s raw score is also considered when determining eligibility. “The raw scores—maybe I could have shown you the data—you would find that somebody got one, somebody got 10 out of 100, somebody got 12 or 20 out of 100, and that qualifies as a failure,” he explained. Meanwhile, the CSSPS has activated call centres to address placement-related complaints and assist candidates and parents who may be unable to visit regional resolution centres. Mr Sulemana said those seeking assistance could contact the call centres and explain their challenges for the necessary support. “If you are in a district far from the regional centre, all you have to do is call the call centre, let them understand your issue, and that will be resolved for you,” he said.

items.title: L’Europe commande à Bull le supercalculateur LUMI-AI pour 387,8 millions d’euros
items.description: EuroHPC a confié à Bull la livraison de LUMI-AI, un supercalculateur prévu en Finlande au second semestre 2027. Le contrat de 387,8 millions d’euros couvre l’acquisition, l’installation et la maintenance, avec une capacité d’IA annoncée dix fois supérieure à celle du système LUMI actuel. L’Europe engage 387,8 millions d’euros pour renforcer ses capacités de calcul consacrées à l’intelligence artificielle. L’entreprise française Bull a été choisie par l’entreprise commune EuroHPC et la LUMI AI Factory pour construire LUMI-AI. Le contrat couvre l’acquisition, la livraison, l’installation et la maintenance. Le futur système appartiendra à EuroHPC et sera installé dans le centre de données de CSC, à Kajaani, en Finlande. La mise en service est programmée pour le second semestre 2027. Les responsables du projet annoncent une capacité de calcul pour l’IA multipliée par dix et une puissance de calcul haute performance presque doublée par rapport au supercalculateur LUMI actuel. Ces comparaisons décrivent un objectif de conception; les performances réelles devront être mesurées après l’installation, sur des applications et des conditions d’utilisation définies. La machine reposera sur des accélérateurs AMD Instinct MI430X de nouvelle génération et des processeurs AMD EPYC de sixième génération comptant 256 cœurs. Bull fournira également son interconnexion BXI et un refroidissement direct par eau chaude. L’infrastructure doit servir à l’entraînement et à l’exécution de modèles d’IA, au calcul scientifique et à l’analyse de grands volumes de données. Elle formera le socle informatique de la LUMI AI Factory, destinée aux entreprises, aux chercheurs et aux organismes publics européens. Le volet énergétique occupe une place centrale dans le projet. Les promoteurs annoncent une alimentation électrique entièrement renouvelable. La chaleur récupérée dans le centre de données doit rejoindre le réseau de chauffage urbain de Kajaani. Cette architecture peut réduire une partie de l’énergie perdue sous forme de chaleur, mais le communiqué ne publie pas encore la consommation électrique totale du futur système, son efficacité mesurée en exploitation ni la quantité de chaleur effectivement valorisée. LUMI-AI prolonge les investissements européens dans des capacités de calcul accessibles sur le continent. Le montant annoncé donne une mesure plus complète que le seul prix des machines puisqu’il inclut plusieurs étapes du contrat et la maintenance. Les sources consultées ne détaillent toutefois pas la répartition entre matériel, logiciels, travaux, exploitation et durée exacte de maintenance. Le projet devra aussi préciser comment seront partagées les ressources entre recherche publique, entreprises établies et jeunes pousses, ainsi que les règles applicables aux données sensibles. Le calendrier dépendra de la disponibilité des composants, de la préparation du nouveau centre de données de Renforsin Ranta et des essais de réception. Les critères d’accès pour les entreprises et les équipes de recherche devront être précisés par la LUMI AI Factory avant l’ouverture effective du service. Cet article vous est proposé en collaboration avec Aïobi . Contact : team@aiobi.world L’article L’Europe commande à Bull le supercalculateur LUMI-AI pour 387,8 millions d’euros est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

Based on the figures provided, about 55,000 candidates will be excluded from the placement exercise. Mr Sulemana acknowledged that obtaining Grade 9 under the standardised grading system did not automatically mean that a candidate had failed. He explained, however, that the candidates’ raw scores were also considered when determining their eligibility. “The raw scores—maybe I could have shown you the data—you would find that somebody got one, somebody got 10 out of 100, somebody got 12 or 20 out of 100, and that qualifies as a failure,” he said. The CSSPS Coordinator also disclosed that only about 17 per cent of the candidates, representing approximately 107,000 students, obtained aggregates ranging from six to 18. “If you look at the data on the performance of the candidates, we only had about 17 per cent of the candidates getting from aggregate six to 18. In absolute figures, you are talking about 107,000,” he said. He added that approximately 252,000 candidates, representing about 35 per cent of the total, obtained aggregates ranging from six to 24. Meanwhile, the CSSPS has activated its call centres to address complaints and other challenges that may arise during the placement exercise. Mr Sulemana said candidates and parents who live far from regional resolution centres could contact the call centres for assistance. “If you are in a district far from the regional centre, all you have to do is call the call centre, let them understand your issue, and that will be resolved for you,” he said.

items.description: © DR Le 1er septembre 2026 à Yaoundé, le ministre Henri Eyebe Ayissi a présidé les assises spéciales sur la réforme foncière, annonçant l'application immédiate des lettres-circulaires 2024-2026 et la lettre-circulaire n°0005 du 31 août dernier sur les Commissions consultatives. Le Conseil régional du Centre a abrité le 1er septembre 2026, les assises spéciales consacrées au lancement officiel des lettres-circulaires et instructions ministérielles 2024-2026 pour la gouvernance foncière. Le ministre a rappelé les limites de l'ordonnance de 1974 face à la pression démographique, l'urbanisation et les contentieux, et justifié la réforme engagée dans le cadre de la SND30 et des directives de la FAO. Deux annonces majeures : la signature de la Lettre-Circulaire n°0005 du 31 août 2026 fixant les modalités de désignation des notables au sein des Commissions Consultatives, et une évaluation rigoureuse lors du débat parlementaire sur le futur projet de loi foncier. Le MINDCAF a prescrit l'application stricte et immédiate : fichier annuel actualisé des attestations des chefferies de 3e degré, barèmes de descente des commissions et soumission de tous les dossiers en cours aux nouvelles règles, sous peine de sanctions. items.title: 2026 National Cyber Security Awareness Month launched to build digital trust
items.description: The Cyber Security Authority (CSA), together with key public and private-sector partners, has launched the 2026 National Cyber Security Awareness Month (NCSAM), calling for stronger collaboration to secure Ghana’s rapidly expanding digital finance ecosystem.The month-long campaign, running from October 1 to 31, 2026, is being held under the theme ‘Securing Ghana’s Digital Finance Ecosystem: Building Trust Through Collaboration and Cyber Resilience’. The launch at CalBank’s head office auditorium in Accra marked a renewed commitment by regulators, law enforcement, financial institutions and other stakeholders to strengthen cybersecurity, combat cyber-enabled fraud and build public confidence in digital financial services. The partners also emphasised the need to move cybersecurity beyond a compliance requirement and make it a shared governance, business and national resilience priority. Speaking at the event, CSA Director-General, Mr. Divine Selase Agbeti, said the theme reflects the growing cyber risks accompanying the rapid expansion of digital financial services.Citing the BoG’s 2025 Fraud Report, Mr. Agbeti said fraud cases recorded across banks, specialised deposit-taking institutions and payment service providers increased by 48 percent, from 16,733 in 2024 to 24,778 in 2025. Electronic fraud incidents in the payment service provider segment also rose by 54 percent. The CSA recorded 3,876 cybersecurity incidents between January and July 2026, with online fraud accounting for approximately 47 percent.“Cybersecurity cannot remain a compliance exercise done solely for the regulator, a technology project dedicated solely to the IT department, or an expense deferred until after an incident. It is a duty owed to every customer whose money and data you hold,” Mr. Agbeti said. He urged banks, fintechs, payment service providers, insurers and merchants to procure cybersecurity services only from providers licensed or accredited by the CSA, in line with Ghana’s cybersecurity regulatory framework.“The Authority will exercise the powers available to it when institutions or service providers disregard applicable cybersecurity obligations and put the public at risk,” he cautioned. Chief Risk Officer of CalBank PLC, Mr. Sadiq Atta, who delivered welcome remarks on behalf of the Managing Director, Mr. Carl Selasi Asem, said the campaign theme was particularly relevant to the financial sector as digital adoption expands both opportunities and exposure to cyber risk. “Our task, therefore, is not to hold back innovation; it is to pursue innovation in a way that strengthens security, resilience and trust,” he said. Mr. Atta called for closer collaboration among regulators, financial institutions, law-enforcement agencies, technology providers, academia, the media and the public, noting that no single institution can secure the digital ecosystem alone. Mr Divine Selase Agbeti, Director General, Cyber Security Authority addresses the audience present at the media launch of the Cyber Security Awareness Month (NCSAM) 2026 Five strategic pillars Delivering the keynote address on behalf of the Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Hon. Samuel Nartey George, Deputy Minister Hon. Mohammed Adams Sukparu outlined five strategic pillars for NCSAM 2026: Securing Ghana’s digital finance ecosystem Cybercrime prevention and response Cyber resilience and critical infrastructure protection Cyber hygiene; the basic, routine practices people and organisations follow to keep their devices, accounts, systems and data secure from cyber threats and digital safety Capacity building, research and multi-stakeholder collaboration. Mr. Sukparu said the initiative seeks to build confidence in Ghana’s digital economy. “Let us build a Ghana where a citizen can make a digital payment with confidence, where a business can innovate without unnecessary fear, and where investors can have confidence in the resilience of our digital economy,” he said. Cyber Security Authority (CSA) The Cyber Security Authority (CSA) is Ghana’s national regulator for cybersecurity, established under the Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038), and operational since October 1, 2021. The Authority is responsible for regulating cybersecurity activities, preventing and responding to cybersecurity threats and incidents, protecting Critical Information Infrastructure, and promoting a secure and resilient digital ecosystem. As a government agency under the Ministry of Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, the CSA works with public and private-sector institutions, law-enforcement agencies, industry, academia and international partners to strengthen cybersecurity, deter cybercrime, build national capacity and promote cybersecurity awareness. Its regulatory responsibilities include licensing Cybersecurity Service Providers, accrediting Cybersecurity Establishments and Professionals, overseeing cybersecurity requirements for Critical Information Infrastructure, coordinating national incident response through CERT-GH, and promoting public education and cyber safety. The CSA also leads national cybersecurity awareness initiatives, including the annual National Cyber Security Awareness Month (NCSAM), as part of its broader mandate to build a secure and resilient digital Ghana. For cybersecurity incident reporting and advice, the public can contact the CSA on 292.

items.title: Disney star Carla Jeffery dies at 33
items.description: Carla Jeffery, the actress known for playing Bree in Disney’s popular Zombies film franchise, has died at the age of 33. Jeffery’s death was confirmed by her manager, Carla Alexander, founder of Los Angeles-based Alexanders Talent Management. “Carla was more than a client; she was family,” Alexander said in a statement. “Our hearts are with Carla’s family and loved ones during this devastating time.” Alexander told KTLA that further details about the actress’s death would be released in the coming days. Her cause of death has not been disclosed. Born in Houston, Texas, Jeffery began her acting career at the age of 12, appearing alongside Mo’Nique in the 2006 comedy film Phat Girlz. She later featured in several Disney Channel productions, including Good Luck Charlie, Shake It Up! and Best Friends Whenever. Jeffery gained wider recognition for her role as Bree in Disney’s Zombies franchise. Her character was portrayed as a close and loyal friend to Addison, played by Meg Donnelly, and became a familiar face to fans throughout the film series and its animated spinoff. Beyond Zombies, Jeffery also appeared in other film and television projects, including Disney’s Prom Pact. Reflecting on the actress, Alexander said, “She loved what she did. She was a great person.” Jeffery’s death has prompted an outpouring of grief from fans and colleagues who remembered her for her work and contributions to Disney’s young-adult entertainment projects. The post Disney star Carla Jeffery dies at 33 appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Le CFCM accuse l’extrême droite d’alimenter les divisions autour du voile
items.description: Le débat sur le port du voile en France s’est de nouveau invité au cœur de la confrontation politique. Le Conseil français du culte musulman (CFCM) a exhorté les responsables politiques à cesser de prendre les musulmans pour cible, après la proposition du Rassemblement national (RN) de sanctionner financièrement les femmes portant le voile dans l’espace public en cas d’arrivée du parti au pouvoir. Dans un communiqué, le CFCM dénonce des déclarations qu’il juge « irresponsables » et estime que l’assimilation des femmes musulmanes voilées à des courants extrémistes contribue à leur désignation comme boucs émissaires. L’organisation souligne que ces femmes sont déjà exposées à des insultes, des menaces, des intimidations et parfois à des agressions. Cette réaction intervient après les propos de Jean-Philippe Tanguy, député et proche collaborateur de Marine Le Pen. Celui-ci a indiqué que le Rassemblement national envisageait d’instaurer des amendes à l’encontre des femmes portant le voile dans les lieux publics si la présidente du groupe remportait l’élection présidentielle de 2027. Le parti présente cette mesure comme un volet de sa lutte contre ce qu’il qualifie « d’idéologie islamiste ». Face à cette perspective, le CFCM rappelle que le voile ne peut être réduit à une manifestation d’idéologies radicales contemporaines. Selon lui, le port d’un couvre-chef ou d’un voile est attesté depuis des siècles dans les traditions juive, chrétienne et musulmane, où il renvoie à des références religieuses et morales anciennes. L’institution considère que l’appropriation du voile par certains mouvements extrémistes ne modifie en rien sa dimension religieuse. Elle juge dès lors injustifiable toute volonté d’interdire ce vêtement dans l’espace public pour les femmes qui choisissent de le porter librement, par conviction religieuse ou personnelle. Le Conseil estime par ailleurs que la République doit garantir de manière égale les droits des femmes qui portent le voile et de celles qui choisissent de ne pas le porter, dans le respect de la liberté individuelle et de la liberté de conscience. Au-delà de la question du voile, le CFCM critique l’introduction du contrôle vestimentaire des femmes dans le débat électoral. Il juge inapproprié de mobiliser les forces de l’ordre pour surveiller la tenue des citoyennes alors que la France fait face à des enjeux sécuritaires d’une tout autre ampleur. L’organisation rappelle que les moyens des services de sécurité devraient prioritairement être consacrés à la lutte contre le terrorisme, la criminalité, le trafic de stupéfiants, les violences et les différentes formes d’insécurité, plutôt qu’à la surveillance de l’habillement dans l’espace public. Le Conseil met également en garde contre une instrumentalisation des peurs dans le cadre de la compétition électorale. Selon lui, les discours fondés sur la division et la désignation d’une partie de la population comme problème politique risquent de détourner l’attention des difficultés économiques et sociales auxquelles sont confrontés les Français. Réaffirmant son opposition à toute interdiction générale du voile dans les espaces publics, le CFCM soutient qu’une telle mesure serait contraire aux principes républicains, notamment la liberté de conscience, les libertés individuelles et la laïcité. Il avertit également qu’une législation visant une catégorie spécifique de citoyens pourrait favoriser la discrimination, la haine et les violences. Pour étayer son argumentation, l’institution invoque les prises de position d’Aristide Briand lors des débats précédant l’adoption de la loi de 1905 sur la séparation des Églises et de l’État. Elle rappelle que l’homme politique français mettait déjà en garde contre des dispositions susceptibles d’exposer la République à des accusations d’intolérance, alors que l’ambition première du texte était d’établir un « régime de liberté ». En conclusion, le Conseil français du culte musulman appelle les responsables politiques à faire preuve de responsabilité et de discernement. Il invite également les citoyens attachés aux valeurs de liberté, d’égalité et de fraternité à prendre part au débat public afin de contrer les discours de division, tout en refusant que « des millions de Français deviennent les otages de stratégies électoralistes ». « Ne prenons pas pour cible les femmes musulmanes », conclut-il. Douala a abrité les 1er et 2 septembre 2026, la 11e édition des Caravanes de sensibilisation des PME pour leur adhésion aux Centres de Gestion Agréés (CGA). Placée sous le thème « Optimisation du dispositif d'accompagnement des entrepreneurs dans les CGA : défis, stratégies et perspectives », cette initiative du Ministère des PME, de l'Économie Sociale et de l'Artisanat vise à rapprocher les entrepreneurs des dispositifs d'accompagnement pour favoriser formalisation, gouvernance et pérennisation. Au cœur des échanges : avantages liés à l'adhésion aux CGA, obligations comptables et fiscales, nouvelles mesures de la Loi de finances 2026, réforme de la fiscalité locale et Impôt Général Synthétique, accès au financement et accompagnement des jeunes et femmes entrepreneurs. L'écosystème était mobilisé : administrations, DGI, structures d'appui, patronat, banques, chambres consulaires, CGA et partenaires techniques. Objectif : sensibiliser 5 000 acteurs. La caravane s'est déployée à travers un village des CGA, une caravane mobile dans la ville et des descentes chez un jeune et une femme entrepreneure. Depuis 2016, le MINPMEESA poursuit cette dynamique à travers le pays. Cet article PME : Douala accueille la 11e Caravane des CGA est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Davido hits back at Erigga over ‘family money’ tweet
items.description: Nigerian music star David Adeleke, popularly known as Davido, has responded to rapper Erigga after the latter praised musicians who built their careers without financial backing from wealthy families. Erigga, whose real name is Erhiga Agarivbie, sparked the conversation in a post on X, where he wrote, “Shoutout to all the musicians who don’t come from family money and had to grind for every single dollar they earn.” Although Erigga did not mention any artiste by name, his post generated reactions online, with many interpreting it as a comment on musicians who came from privileged backgrounds. Davido subsequently quoted the post and offered a different perspective, arguing that musicians from wealthy families can also deserve recognition for working hard to establish themselves. He wrote, “No be we say make your pops no guard o. Shoutout to the ones that came from family money and still grind to the top.” The exchange later escalated, with Davido describing Erigga’s message as “useless motivation” and referring to him as an “imbecile.” The Afrobeats star also appeared to suggest that he could eventually leave music and focus on his other financial interests. “No worry o I go soon leave their music for una go make my billions… then that shit gonna be boring AF,” he wrote. Davido also questioned the perception of poverty, asking, “Deep down, who like poverty?” The exchange has since generated mixed reactions on social media, with some users backing Erigga’s emphasis on artistes who rose without family wealth, while others agreed with Davido that coming from a wealthy background does not automatically diminish an artiste’s hard work or achievements. The post Davido hits back at Erigga over ‘family money’ tweet appeared first on Vanguard News .
